Question: If you are rejected by Amazon, Microsoft, Facebook, and Google for an SDE position, when else can you reapply?
Answer: TL;DR: You will have to wait. Every FAANG (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, Google) company - and Microsoft - has a different policy on how long to wait, which they would have communicated with you. Work accordingly, ideally with the same recruiter who worked with you in the first attempt. But the second time around, prepare really really really well as a third chance may be much more difficult to come by (contrary to popular belief). Longer answer: Rejection is normal. Expect it, accept it - it’s a part of the process of getting in. There’s a well known anecdote about how as a software engineer with 9 years under his belt, Brian Acton interviewed with Twitter and Facebook only to be rejected. With his favorite companies not hiring him, he teamed up with an ex-colleague to start WhatsApp, a company that Facebook eventually, and ironically, bought for $16 billion and then he served on the board of Facebook :-) Talk about revenge :-). The other famous jobsnub story is of Homebrew creator Max Howell and his Google rejection. He explains how he went through 7 interviews before the rejection, despite being a successful software developer, and ironically the creator of a software that Google uses extensively! There are plenty of stories of how some of the smartest people have failed at interviews with top companies. It’s also why we, at Interview Kickstart, like to think of an interview more as a date than a test . You should be prepared for rejection. Ultimately, you only want only one interview that will work. You should also know that most people who are rejected have been successful in their second attempt. These interviews often take a second attempt to even understand what's required of you. It's part of the process; it's normal to be rejected. Many go back, reapply and successfully nail the interview the second time around. The reason for this is in what they do differently between the first and the second time. If you don’t want a second rejection, don’t reapply in a hurry. And with one rejection behind you, it makes sense to prepare for it. You may think there are many who clear interviews with ease but you may be unaware of the effort behind-the-scenes. Some are born genius, some may get lucky, but luck isn’t strategy. You must give interview prep the time it needs. Hiring teams at top tier companies are very driven and want people like themselves. You can’t game the system or fool them. You have to show that you care about your craft and are in it for the right reasons. That has to come through when you meet them. And it’s not going to happen from reading a book for a few days or solving a few problems online. Apply when you are ready because a second rejection will take you further away from your dream company. When should you reapply? When you hear back from the recruiter with a rejection, you can ask them about reapplying because different companies have their own policies about this. Depending on how your interviews went, it could be three months if they feel you could be a potential hire, or 2 years if you destroyed their faith in humanity! Why you only have very few attempts with a company. Reading between the lines: The ATS Most companies, and certainly all the FAANG companies, use an ATS or Applicant Tracking System. Everytime you apply, the ATS notes it. Your resume is on the ATS. If you have interviewed with the company before, the recruiter’s notes and all the interviewers’ notes will be on record along with the decision made on your hiring. Details of your interviews are memorialised in the ATS. And even if the recruiter has changed, the ATS remembers everything! You can’t game the ATS by changing your email id or how you write your name (middle name first, first name later etc). If your social security number has been collected as part of the data, there’s no hiding from it. The crux of the matter is that you need to give the interview the time it needs. It’s not about cracking an interview. Leveling up doesn’t happen overnight. Take your time, prepare, reapply and then go for it. But don’t wait indefinitely because every month that you wait and delay joining a top company, it’s money lost and opportunity lost. Even an increase in $50k in your salary will cost you $4.5k a month. So, start working on it and get to a point of confidence. Question: What do interviewers look for when interviewing software engineering candidates?
Answer: An interviewer is usually evaluating you for three things: i) Do you have the skills? ii) Are you a problem solver? iii) Are you someone I/my team can work with? A tech interview can take between 45 minutes to an hour. Over an hour is generally a good sign. One of the first things that will be noted is your demeanor, and the interviewer will pick on any hints they get - are you shy, timid, confident, involved, apathetic etc. Unless the interviewer wants to jump in straight away (this happens often and can throw you off), there will be some small talk that may involve a couple of tricky questions like: - I haven't had a chance to look at your resume. Can you fill me in on the highlights? - How do you think your other interviews have gone? (If you've had other interviews with the team before this one.) The first question has several variations (“Tell me something about yourself.”) and you’re likely to have been asked a few (100?) times if you've given many interviews. It's important to make sure that your answer is crisp and short. Don't ramble on about where you went to school and other obvious details from your resume. Instead, make it a story that talks more about what lies between the lines on your resume - what your experience has taught you, an example of a tough problem you've solved, what you could bring to the table or even the team you are interviewing with. The second question is trickier. Your personal perception of how things went might be completely different from feedback the interviewer may have already received before walking into the room. The easiest way to tackle this is, to be honest without being either emphatic or vague. You may want to avoid a response like, "They went great" or "I think I killed it". But neither should you take the other extreme, with an "I did terrible in <insert round/problem>". Keep it as neutral, like this: "I think I solved the first question on finding the longest subsequence well but stumbled a little bit on the design problem. I think I could have done better with a little more time." These questions offer the interviewer useful insights about you, and convey the impression that you are secure and comfortable with the good and the bad, and more importantly, that you are the sort of person they'd like to work with. On to the main course - the technical questions. Technical interviewers generally bring two questions to the table. The first: A coding problem to test your knowledge of fundamental data structures and algorithms, something they expect you to solve reasonably quickly (say in 20 mins). The second: A more abstract question that tests your ability to break down a problem and identify a way to solve the problem. This could be a system design question (Design YouTube) or a more focussed question (Design data models for a video streaming service that should be able to stream to multiple devices and support up to a billion users a month). Your interview is usually over if you struggle with the first question. We may not be exposed to core data structures and algorithms in our day job but top companies use that as a minimum benchmark to move you ahead in the interview process. These problems usually test your knowledge of time and space complexity (think Big "O"), your ability to quickly assess what is efficient (and inefficient), and most importantly to write clean code on the whiteboard/coding platform being used. Your evaluation on the second question is mostly based on - How quickly do you break a problem down and figure out what pieces need more clarification? - What follow up questions do you ask the interviewer to get more information? - How well can you articulate your thought process? - Your ability to make tradeoffs and to justify them. - Your ability to offer ballpark estimates for memory, disk space, network load, buffer sizes, etc. The deeper you get into the second question, the better your interview is going because you are challenging the interviewer to throw more at you. On both technical questions, you are being evaluated for all of these: - Articulating your thoughts (GOOD) - Rambling contradictory thoughts (BAD) - Follow up questions and telling the interviewer the direction you are going (GOOD) - Long unexplained silence (BAD) - Organized whiteboard showing assumptions, estimates and linking them to how you are solving the problem (GOOD) - Completely messy whiteboard with no coherence (BAD) - Interviewer throwing newer and more challenges at you than hints (GOOD) - The opposite of the above (BAD) The key to all of these interviews is to be prepared. Companies, at least the coveted tech companies, expect you to prepare before their interviews. It is important to give yourself enough time to practice hard and solve as many different types of questions, know your resume in detail and hone your personal narrative well enough to give yourself the best chance. If you are looking for a structured way to prepare for interviews, take a look at Interview Kickstart.

Question: Are you expected to write the perfect code on your first attempt in tech interviews?
Answer: Nope. Not even at top-tier tech companies. Even your interviewer is unlikely to have written perfect code at first shot in every interview. Heck, even Steph Curry get the basket every time. Interviews are not standardized tests, like the online coding websites have made us believe. Interviews are closer to a date than to a test, and dating has no standards written anywhere to be followed. (Not that anyone will follow them even if they are written). Interviews are not robotic processes that some frustrated blogs have made us believe. Interviews are a very human process which are as much dependent on the interviewers as they are on you and your preparation. For humans, it’s practically impossible to write perfect code at first shot in all interviews. Some interviews, yes. All, no. What is expected though, is the following, which you’ll note is far more human and yet manages to maintain high standards: If writing perfect code at first shot is not expected, then is it okay to take it easy in our prep? Not really. Interviews do need speed, but not inhuman robotic speed. As long as an easy problem is complete within 20 minutes, a medium one within 30 and a hard one within 40, we’re good. Are there exceptions? Are there interviewers who DO care about giving perfect working code in first shot? Yes, there are. After all, interviews are like a date. Are they everywhere in majority? No. Relax. Prepare systematically with the right rigor and right people and you’ll be fine. We’ve seen that with over a thousand engineers we’ve trained.

Question: What tends to trip people up the most in tech interviews?
Answer: Trip up the most in interviews? Communication skills. You see, as software engineers, we spend so much time in front of a computer to get things done, it often reinforces our thinking that communication skills are less important than technical skills. It’s just the opposite. Most projects fail[1] because of a lack of proper communication. The same goes for interviews. Since communication nuances can be subtle, in interviews, it’s more severe than projects because you often don’t get feedback right away or a chance to explain yourself. On the flip side, when the candidate is on the borderline, having demonstrated excellent soft skills turns the benefit of doubt in their favor. Having closely trained nearly 1600+ candidates, here are some related observations from our interview-prep programs: 0. Many resumes of students coming into the program have typos. Serious typos. When you have typos in your resume, you often don’t even get an interview. Of course, the interviewer can overlook the typos, and some will or some won’t even find out in rapid scanning. But many many interviewers tend to be detail-oriented people, working in value-protecting areas of tech, and odds of them missing typos on your resume, are stacked against you. Especially if you have many. Case in point: Lessons from a year’s worth of hiring data For the most part, you had ample time to create your resume and look over it. There are also very good tools available today to correct your mistakes. You have no reason to send one with typos. You shouldn’t be surprised if you don’t get an interview due to that. 1. A large majority of incoming candidates struggle to put together a short elevator pitch about themselves. A simple question of ‘tell me about yourself’ very commonly leads into a 5 minute rambling with no conclusion. An unclear pitch tells the interviewer you don’t know what you want and how your career has progressed. 2. Many candidates find it difficult to articulate why they want to join a certain company. Look, we get it. You just want a job, and the interviewer doesn’t want to be there either. Or well, the answer is obvious - who doesn’t want to join Google? But that’s not how you can come across in an interview! You must articulate intelligently what the company does that you connect with. Things that excite you. Yes, it’s more or less a courtesy, but it’s critical because interviewers are risk-averse in that hour, by definition. If you don’t even do that courtesy, you can come off as clueless or just opportunistic. 3. Many candidates don’t ask questions at the end of their interview. Realize that this is the only time before you make your decision when you have access to core engineers of the company/team, spending an hour each with you. It’s a goldmine. You should be prepared with solid questions to understand as much you can about the culture, the tech-stack, the org chart, and everything else in between. Yes, even if the interview didn’t go well. Why not? That will be very useful to you in making your final decision, whichever company you join. If you don’t ask questions, you come across as either very disinterested, or worse, clueless and arrogant. 4. Here is a more subtle one: So many candidates don’t take hints even when they struggle to solve a given problem in the interview. As an interviewer, when you struggle in an interview, I see that. When you work a little too much, I feel like giving a hint. When I give you a hint, you should take it, even if you don’t agree with it, or even if you didn’t ask for it. Having a quick discussion with me about your current approach and its work is just respectful. Doesn’t take too long. If you don’t do that and I’m not watchful about my thoughts (often interviewers are not!), then I’ll walk out with an unpleasant feeling of being ignored by you. Seems childish on the interviewers’ part? Maybe, but if you do that to two interviewers on the pane, that is flagged as a negative pattern, and the interview is lost. So you see, however well prepared you are on the technical side (which is not trivial either), it’s very easy to trip up on communication nuances. Whenever you look under the hood of failures in interviews, almost always, it’s the lack of introspection, not the absence of coding speed. Almost always, it’s the verbal expression, not expressive code. Almost always, it’s the pitch, not LinkedIn or resume. Almost always, it’s people, not tech. Footnotes [1] Poor communication causes most project management failures | Cutting Edge PR Insights: Boost Your Career

Question: What are some traps in salary negotiation laid by employers?
Answer: Oh, we’ve seen so many of them at Interview Kickstart. Especially for Software Engineers. Biggest trap is asking about your current compensation*. If you clearly reveal what you make right now, then they know what is your “current worth”. They can then just offer you a bit more than that, and you’d be tempted to accept it. [Sometimes they will give you a bit less than that, if the employer considers themselves better than your current one]. Another trap, is instilling FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out) in you. Very often, they do that by telling you that if you accept the offer, then they want to stop offering it to other candidates. Sometimes it’s by presenting an exploding offer (see below). Yet another trap, is dangling a carrot with an exploding offer. They make you a mediocre offer first, and then say they will sweeten it slightly if you sign right away (or by a certain deadline in a few hours). A more sophisticated trap, is to send you congratulations’ notes from all your interviewers and even send you gifts home while you’re thinking about their offer. Idea is to make you focus on how “nice” they are, and less on numbers. There are more. Generally, employers always have a trap available for every negotiation :-) *In California, USA, it’s now illegal to ask for current compensation. But recruiters still find ways out to get to ballpark.

Question: How do I tell my interviewer that ''I don't know that but I can easily look it up in the web?” I'm conceptually weak, but when a given a task and some time I can achieve good results. I learn by diving into the problem directly. How do I sell myself?
Answer: Think about it. Question never is whether you can simply learn something new. Those who want, will, when put on a problem, given enough time. Question always is - how quickly can you learn in that time? How deep can you go in the same time compared to others? And in the process, do you get along with everyone else, or do you cause too much collateral damage? This is what interviewers are trying to find out in an interview, at the very core of it. To do things fast, conceptual clarity is critical to have. Having prior conceptual clarity gets you closer to “good results” faster. And in the same amount of time, it moves you further from just “good results” to “great results” (deeper). So while I’m glad you admitted your weakness, you shouldn’t stop there. Strive to seek conceptual clarity before you try to sell yourself. Yes, seeking conceptual clarity is not easy. It’s hard work, but is entirely worth it.

Question: How many times can you acceptably postpone a Google interview?
Answer: (Putting my Google recruiter hat on). Okay, there is no magic number, I’ll admit. But if I’m your recruiter, I’ll give you upto three (3) times. In my experience, here is how most requests go: First request: You want to prepare. Understandable. I thought so. I’m glad even. Second request: Well, again, okay. Things come up, I understand. Sometimes prep takes longer. Sometimes life gets in the way. Third request: Okay, now it looks like you’re not that interested in us after all at this time. So I’ll let you be. I’ll be here whenever you’re ready. Each time you call, I’ll listen to your reasons. I’ll empathize, but I’ll make you feel ever so slightly bad about it (after all, it’s Google who pays me). But I’ll give you due time. I’ll listen. I won’t react, because I know that pushing you into an interview when you’re not ready, is not worth our time either. But to tell you the truth, I don’t really care that much about you. Earlier when we talked, I may have made you feel like you’re THE engineer Google is waiting for, but in reality, you’re just a number to me. I’ll move on to my next call. I do 16 a day. On an average. And there are thousands like me. (Removing my Google recruiter hat) I’ve never been a Google recruiter, but I’ve hired and worked with many at top-tier companies. I know a lot about how the machine works. In summary, don’t feel too bad postponing your interview. You, a lone engineer, don’t matter to them as much as they make you believe. And Google will always be hiring engineers. If in the remote chance they stop hiring engineers before you’re ready for interviews, then … well, why would you want to work for a company that stops growing?

Question: Can Google waive the coding interview for a software engineer role? I have a PhD from a top school. Although my coding is great, I just don't believe in those useless coding questions.
Answer: Yes; if your reputation precedes you (e.g. with a strong referral from someone influential within Google, or a great piece of public work), then they may waive the phone-screen for you. But that’s about it. If you’re interviewing in the Software Engineering ladder (or any of the adjacent ladders) from L3 (Entry level) through L8 (Director), they’ll not waive the interviews onsite, coding or otherwise. Not even if you are an author of some of the most used software on the planet, no. Being a PhD from a top school is neither a necessary, nor a sufficient criterion for Google. But why won’t they? Google interviews thousands of engineers each week. They need to have a standardized interview process to deal with that kind of volume. It’s extremely difficult to make defendable exceptions at that scale. Especially in entry-level roles. To fill that volume, Google can’t necessarily be looking for people from top schools. They must and are just looking for good, generally smart, hard working people. And that doesn’t need a college degree, much less PhD from a top-school. Case in point, there are plenty of people at Google, without even a college on their resume. Note also, that unlike colleges, Google doesn’t charge an application fee to review your application and interview you. They will literally spend thousands of dollars on a single interview without any guarantee to hire you. In that situation, the candidate has no leverage to dictate specifics in the interview process. But I sense that you may be unnecessarily worried about coding interviews. I’ve coached and worked with hundreds of engineers from all kinds of schools in my career to crack into a variety of companies. Given you are at a top school, I can pretty much guarantee that you have the capability to crush those interviews. Nearly all software engineers with patience have that capability. If you’re worried/anxious, having a slow time, or not able to hold motivation for prep, then you just need to consider a class*. Once you clear the interview with flying colors, now you have some leverage. Leverage to negotiate a better offer, leverage to negotiate a team of your choice, leverage to negotiate a location of your choice, leverage to join at a time convenient to you etc. But none of that happens without clearing coding interviews at Google (and most similar companies). No, not even if you come with a PhD in CS from a top-school. * Taking a class for coding interview prep these days is a norm, even if you are good at coding. A comprehensive class trains you to get a strong leg up and you often end up with a better offer in a better role. We can help: Interview Kickstart.

Question: Do things get easy for software engineers at Google and Facebook after they are accepted?
Answer: Do things get easy? Not until you reach what is called a “terminal level” (or the “rest and vest level”) in the corporate ladder. Tough interviews were just a trailer to the movie. After you get in, you’re expected to be promoted to the next level in a few years, usually within three years. Until that happens, you’re under a close watch. After you get your first promotion, they cut you a bit of slack, but not until you reach what I call the “terminal level” (for lack of a better phrase). Terminal level is the level you can retire at if you want. For Software Engineers, it’s often the “Senior Software Engineer” level at most companies. At that level, if you just keep meeting expectations (and not exceed them), then you will generally be fine. Sometimes that’s what your life needs. It’s a level where the work is difficult and nuanced for newcomers to do, but because you have gained expertise in it over a number of years, you can be relied on to do it super well. As long as you keep doing that and keep making necessary fixes, you’re generally fine. That’s about as easy as it gets. Even then, as the company evolves (and in Tech, companies evolve very fast), a lot of work often gets obviated and you have to learn new things to keep up. Or often you get colleagues who don’t want to coast at that level and that makes you feel quite incompetent in comparison. But I think you may be missing the point: Taking it easy is not why you join a top institution. A top institution, by definition, is a place, where very driven people have gravitated and gathered to make an impact against all odds. It’s not meant to be like Hunger Games, but is not easy to survive at one either. It’s not easy to survive at Harvard and Stanford in the US, or IITs in India or Technion in Israel. It’s not easy to survive at Teach For America or Doctors without Borders. It’s not easy to survive as President of a country and it’s not easy to survive in top boarding schools either. Heck, it’s also not easy to survive as an instructor at Interview Kickstart! You join a top institution to make a solid impact with your hands, mind and time, faster than elsewhere. Even if you are there for a short time. It’s a unique opportunity to push yourself and surprise yourself with what you can do in the company of other driven people. If you ever find that it got easy, and lift your head up after coasting a long time, you’ll notice that Google is not Google and Facebook is not Facebook. Some other company would be enjoying the top spot. And guess what - it’d now be much harder for YOU to switch out of Google and Facebook and get into this new top company. Case in point: Cisco, Oracle, IBM and many more. Very few people like you and I, are fortunate enough to get all our ducks in a row to end up working for a top institution. I sincerely hope you make the most of it.

Question: What are some stay/away alarms in a company that a software engineer must not ignore?
Answer: 1. Two consecutive bad quarters Far too many software engineers, despite being how cerebral they are, don’t (or refuse to) pay attention to how the business is doing. Reality of the matter is, that the most beautiful and robust code you write day in and day out, is not going to be useful if the company is not selling well. Every so often, you should walk down to the sales folks (or an executive you trust) and ask how the company did last quarter. Just casually. e.g. You’re looking for happy, smiling faces and somewhat precise answers. e.g. For one quarter (not two) if you get lukewarm answers (or just no answers), that’s an important data-point. Nothing to act on yet, but an important one none-the-less. If you get similar lukewarm answers in the next quarter, then you should start to get alarmed. Your equity, bonus and probably your job, are at risk. Especially if you are a startup. If you are at a big company though, then you can possibly pull on for a full bad year or even two sometimes without growth. But without growth, the working environment becomes dull. Fewer new deals are inked, fewer requests for new features and new systems come, there is more maintenance work etc. 2. Executives leaving back to back If you see members of executive team leaving too fast, then that’s a bad sign. Multiple departures in a matter of 3–6 months is too fast. Executive tenures are usually short (less than 2 years), so longer than 6 months in this case don’t make sense. Executive team is VPs or SVPs or CXOs; anyone close to the CEO. They are abreast of what’s going on and make business-critical day to day decisions. Fast departures signal that Any of these above will come to bite you. 3. A large legacy codebase with many entrenched stewards When you are in a team that has a large legacy codebase that’s maintained/enhanced by a team of engineers who have been at the company for a long time, then you generally have little leeway to make an impact. You’ll learn “new” stuff, but only the arcane legacy ways. Not modern software engineering.

Question: In a coding interview, if you say things like "I don't quite remember the syntax, but…" or "I don't quite know how it is implemented, but…", and is able to provide an answer in plain English and logic, how would the interviewer look upon that?
Answer: Any reasonable interviewer will be fine with that, given you’re not habitually doing it. If you happen to answer like that every time I ask you to go deeper into something, then it starts to get suspicious. If you claim to know one programming language, then I expect that you have an urge to be precise when you express (code) in that language. Notice I didn’t say I expect you to be precise - just an urge to be precise. In other words, it’s very okay to not remember syntax (that’s what IDEs are for), but it’s not okay to just assume that I’ll be fine with it, and move on without checking with me. I need to see you trying to remember syntax and assume a reasonably correct syntax before taking my permission to move on. Handwaving and assuming my agreement is a red flag. It is very okay to not remember how something is implemented, but it’s not okay to say that for everything and not okay to say that for frequently used fundamental building blocks. e.g if you claim to know C++ STL through your work experience, but don’t know that std::map and std::set are implemented with Tree-like access characteristics, then that’s a problem. One very important thing interviewers look for in an interviewee, is an urge to go deeper and have only a few black boxes in systems they use. If the knowledge is surface level only, then it’s usually not very impressive. Especially at top companies. I run a bootcamp, focused on technical interview prep: Interview Kickstart. Previously, I was a Director of Engineering at Box.

Question: What are the interview design questions which do not fall into the system design category?
Answer: Categorization in interview-questions’ landscape, is a bit random. It’s often not possible to clearly tell what is a “system design” question and what is a “coding” question. * Take Concurrency for example. It’s a “system design” question in some ways, because you’re designing a concurrent “system”, or making something multi-threaded when it’s not. But in other ways, in an interview, it boils down to just a piece of code using some concurrency primitives that the OS provides. Is it a design question that doesn’t clearly fit into design category? Maybe. * Take Object Modeling as another example. It is also a “system design” question many would argue, but in an interview, it often boils down to writing a few classes augmented by some diagrams, if at all. So that could be another example. * Take the interview question of Designing Amazon’s Product Review System. On the face of it, it’s probably not even possible to tell what the interviewer is expecting (class design? architecture? UI?). Once you clarify, you may find, that s/he is expecting actual code! And when you start thinking about it, you’ll realize that it boils down to a well-known caching algorithm! So there you go - yet another example. I could go on and on. The point I want to make though, is that it doesn’t really help thinking this way Interviews questions are just that viz. interview questions. Their purpose is to know your thought process, your articulation, your behavioral traits and verify your knowledge/experience. Whether the question comes disguised as a “system design” question or a “coding” question or whatever else, has little relevance. [About me: I run the largest technical interview prep bootcamp[1] in the Bay Area. In our programs, we go deep into various CS topics, which eventually helps tremendously in cracking at top companies and sustaining there]

Question: Why do engineering interviewers ask questions that can easily be Googled, when they also know that most engineers would not have the answer memorized?
Answer: Because we are not looking for answers. We are looking for your thought process in solving problems, and your articulation / behavior during the expression of that thought-process (sometimes that is coding). We prefer algorithmic questions (aka questions that can be Googled) because they have many distinct advantages when it comes to interviews, one of them being easy standardization across a large engineering org. Here[1] is my more detailed treatise on it. Fact is, it rarely if at all, even crosses our minds if something is Googleable or not. A few reasons: I’d go as far as saying, that beyond a certain point, even the question asked has no bearing on interview outcome. A good interviewer, will be able to judge you with m/any questions, not just one or two that are their favorites. Good interviewers look at how intently you listen, what clarifying questions you ask, what paths of thought you take, do you come back from false starts quickly, do you give up too soon, do you care about your code, are you fast enough, do you articulate properly, do you think about efficiency as second nature, do you do proper tradeoffs when there are multiple solutions, do you answer questions thoughtfully or do you wing it, do you need too many hints, do you look for bugs in your own code or are you too arrogant to look for them etc. This kind of process, tells me a lot more about whether I will gel with you at work or not. And good interviewers can do this with most questions, Googleable or not. Ironically, the company Google itself does have a semi-automated process internally to find out if a question has leaked outside, but that’s more of an exception than a norm. [About me: For past 4 years, I have been running the largest and the most comprehensive technical interview prep bootcamp in the US[2]. If anyone wants to permanently up-level to top tier tech companies, then this is the place]

Question: What strategy do you avoid when negotiating your salary?
Answer: Having negotiated hundreds of compensation packages, especially in Software Engineering, here is the key: Avoid negotiating without a comparable competing offer. Except for the top few companies, most companies have limitations on what they can offer for your role. Your goal in a negotiation, is to push them to their limits. Your goal is not to get a specific number you have in mind. And unless the company fears missing out on you, they are very unlikely to give you the best they have to offer. There is a small chance that withholding/faking/sweet-talking specific info can give you a bump, but nothing gives you the kind of jumps that having a comparable offer does. Software Engineers are also not very good at withholding/faking/sweet-talking. A much much much better way, is to just get another comparable offer. (I know it’s easier said than done, but then everything worthwhile is). Realize that the other offer needs to be comparable. e.g. Google won’t negotiate with a random startup down the street, but it will negotiate for Facebook or even Amazon or Apple. Remember, how companies tell you that you must accept/reject this offer by this day, otherwise they will go with “other candidates”? And remember how you get so enticed/agonized to accept after they tell you that? You do the same thing to them. My boss had once told me: If you can’t walk away from a deal, you don’t have the deal on your terms. He was 100% right. For last 4+ years, I run the largest bootcamp for technical interview prep for top companies: InterviewKickstart. We routinely negotiate compensation at various companies for our candidates. It’s so much fun :-)

Question: Are there really engineers making 300k+ in Silicon Valley?
Answer: It is the truth. Not just $300K, but much more than that. $500K, $600K, $1MM+… Per year. How do I know? What kind of companies make these offers? Every company that values technical talent very highly, is willing to make these offers. They have to, because they are competing with each other for the same talent. Company size/stage doesn’t matter. Tiny companies have made these offers and giants have too. Location doesn’t matter these days either. Most of these are colocated in California, NY, and Seattle, but we’ve seen these in Michigan and Oklahoma too. Both, tech and non-tech companies have given out these offers. e.g. Ford, a manufacturing company of many generations, has now realized that without self-driving, they are doomed. They are now willing to pay top dollar for that talent. When the leadership values core tech as a critical part of the business, they will open up the wallet. How much experience is required to get these offers? Generally, we see such high offers only for experienced engineers. About 5 years+ of software development experience is required. It is rare for fresh/recent grads (and for new entrants into programming) to get these numbers, unless of course, you come with a strong pedigree e.g. Stanford CS. No, you don’t need a PhD, or even an MS. Is it all cash? No. Up to about $500K, it’s usually half cash (including bonus), half equity. Beyond that, equity dominates. Equity may not feel as exciting as cash, but consider this: How do I prepare to get these offers? (which I think, is the real question you’re asking): A few months of hard work, a lifetime of gravy. It’s the best of times; it’s the worst of times. [To put this into perspective, 75% of America has saved less than $200K for their entire retirement. Here, we’re talking about 2x to 5x that every year. And this has been going on for at least a decade.]

Question: What should I do as I failed my third and final interview at Google?
Answer: I’m not going to offer you sympathy. But I’ll help you think about this at a higher abstraction. My team and I have trained hundreds of engineers to crack into top-tier companies across the US (including Google, of course). The right way viz. with hard work. We hence have a very good pulse on the hiring of engineers at top-tier companies. With that experience, let me tell you a couple of things that I think are important to realize: 1. Not all smart people go to Google anymore. Google is past its prime. If you continue to crave for Google, you will blindside yourself to other upcoming top companies. There was indeed a time (circa pre-2013?) when Google provided a unique opportunity. It was practically the only tech company where you’d get top-line compensation, where you’d work with very cerebrally smart achievers, work on unique products that needed a lot of upfront investment, and of course, have great free/subsidized food. Not to mention fun interview questions. Google indeed pushed the bar very far from what they got and made an undeniable mark in the history of tech. But as you’d expect, in their battle for survival, other companies started to catch up. Some have even exceeded what Google currently offers. After all, Google is a 20+ years old company; a previous generation company. There are cases of father and son duo working for Google these days. You probably already know some usual suspects e.g. Facebook. Netflix. There is also a slew of awesome startups/pre-IPO/recently-IPOed companies that offer you the same deal now. e.g. Quora itself. There are many more names I can give you. Names of companies working on very interesting, challenging tech products and growing fast. Same companies also offer free/subsidized food. And the same ones also pay top-line compensation. And of course, the same companies also ask difficult interview questions. And oh, the same companies are often founded by engineers who have now left Google. And/or they have engineers hired away from Google i.e. you won’t miss the “company” of so-called cerebral folks either. Google isn’t even the most well-known company anymore. Many more chances that your Grandma has heard more of Apple and Amazon more these days, instead of Google. If you’re still not convinced, then take a look at World’s 20 largest tech companies. Google is on the list, but if you think that 19 other companies came this far without having everything else that Google has, then I’m afraid you need to do some more thinking. 2. Work harder. Nobody cares. Not for Google anymore. But for another top-tech company. Yes, there are many more awesome tech companies around. But there is also that much more talent to go around now. It’s not easy. It never was and it never will be. You need to really understand the interview process deeply. You need to work hard to be a good engineer. You need to care about your craft. You need to take pride in your work. You need to surround yourself with positive people and shun negative ones. You need to prepare to show all that in an interview setting. You need to prepare to win. Above all, you need to not give up.

Question: What are some of the most common mistakes people make in job interviews? How can these mistakes be avoided?
Answer: 1. Most common mistake, by far: Going to an interview to look for a job You should not go to an interview to look for a job; instead, you should go to the interview to show what you do and show what you are capable of. Of course, with humility. Nobody explains it better than Bryan Cranson does in this 1-minute impromptu advice: Skipped the video? Don’t. For many, this one minute was life-changing advice. Listen to it, over and over again. 2. Second most common mistake, by far: Going to an interview taking a position of weakness (insecurities), instead of a position of strength What if things go wrong? What if I can’t answer questions that they ask? What if my friends secretly ridicule me if I don’t clear the interview? What if I’m stamped a stupid incapable person by my family, forever? What if this is the last interview I ever have? Clouding your mind with such insecurities is often natural to many many people, especially before an event where they are going to be judged (e.g. an interview) by another person. But they never ever do any good. Self-doubt just weakens your brain-response, and that in turn, ironically leads to low performance in an interview! How to avoid these mistakes? (Both are different, but related). 1. Understand the nature of the beast Before you to go interviews, take a few minutes to understand what they are. And specifically, how they are done for the companies/roles you’re targeting. Interviews are not like standardized tests, where preparation of technical content is the only thing that is required. Interviews are more like a date, where inspiring the other person with who you are and what you can do, matters far more than anything else. Just the way you wouldn’t go to a speed date agonizing about getting into a long-term relationship, you wouldn’t go to an interview agonizing about getting a job. Those who internalize this, do way better than those who don’t. Every company also has a specific process they follow for specific roles. Getting as much information as you can about the process and people involved in the company will also go a long way in avoiding these mistakes. 2. Prepare, prepare, prepare If you are the kind of person who doesn’t have an unshakeable faith in your instincts to support you at the right time in an interview, then you need to prepare beforehand. And prepare well. Put yourself into a similar situation number of times. e.g. Do mock interviews with people on the other side. Seek detailed feedback and calibrate. e.g. Do burner interviews at companies you don’t care to work for. Introspect and seek as much feedback as possible. This way, you’ll substantially get over self-doubt, recognize your own strengths and limitations, leading to very positive outcomes. Everything else will fall in place. Oh, it will. We’ve seen that, over and over again.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What are the typical salary ranges for software engineers at places like Google, Facebook, Twitter, Palantir, et al?
Answer: Tier-1 companies have a WIDE disparity in what software engineers are paid. Their goal in compensation is to not be fair, but be equitable. You’ll never find out typical ranges, because nearly all salary data that you see on public websites, is self-reported and extrapolated with no solid backing. It’s cooked to sell, and just be defensible in case of someone questioning it. Unless one is unscrupulous, there is really just no way to get that accurate data. In order to get the real answers and insights, you need to reach out to people who have experience on both sides i.e. making offers and coaching engineers to get those offers. Like some others, I have that experience. I’ve made many offers to software engineers from my budget at a top-tier company in Silicon Valley. And now I coach software engineers full-time on how to get those life-changing lucrative offers. With that, let me dissect this question and thus answer it: Typical? Don’t chase “typical”. Chase what you can get with who you are. There is nothing typical about a software engineer salary at top tech companies. Nothing at all. I’ve seen $300k total comp for a 15 years’ experienced engineer and $600k total comp for an 8 years’ experienced engineer too. Salary? Don’t chase “salary”. Chase total compensation. At top tech companies, salaries don’t matter as much as equity and bonuses do (total compensation). Salaries are similar everywhere these days in Sillycon valley, whether it’s a 1-year-old VC funded startup, or Amazon. Largest differentiation is in Equity and Bonus. Remember, that Salary merely pays the bills. Bonuses are for vacations and it’s the equity that really makes your retirement (and everything else). Ranges? Don’t chase a “range”. Ranges are laughably vast to be super useful. Here is what we know and what you will find out when you look at the actual numbers first-hand: Entry level to mid-tier: $100k to ~200K Senior Engineer: $200k to ~300k Staff and above: $300 to $1mm+. for software engineers? Do chase software-engineering :-) The demand-supply curve of engineers who are driven is very skewed in favor of engineers. And realize, that it is because the compensation today is not typical that you will be able to get away with outsized numbers these days. Remember this always: Best opportunities only exist when the variance is high. Otherwise you’ll get just what everyone else gets. Go clear that interview and grab it.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What is the difference between a 'data structures and algorithms' interview and a 'coding' one?
Answer: There isn’t any practical difference today; they are synonymous. If you want to be pedantic, you can argue that DS and Algos have independently existed in the world of mathematics for many years, even before coding was a thing. i.e. they should be considered differently from coding. But the fact of the matter is, that for mere mortals like us, DS and Algos don’t exist outside of coding. e.g. There is no use of a Binary Tree in a software engineer’s life if you are not going to code it. As a result, engineers use the two interview-types interchangeably now. Even when there are no interesting DS/Algos involved in an interview question (e.g. fizzbuzz), it’s often called a “DS/Algos” interview, and even when there are core DS/Algos invovled (e.g. find longest repeating substring), people often call it a “coding” interview.

Question: It takes how many hours for a computer science graduate with weak algorithm skills to prepare for the Google interview?
Answer: Obviously, the count of hours is different for different engineers. But here is some anecdotal evidence: 1. The most popular tech interview book in the market, Cracking the coding interview, had 150 problems (until the latest edition, which is 190). Assuming each problem takes an average of one hour (super optimistic), you're looking at ~150+ hours of practice. 2. An algorithms class in a university is about 45 hours in a semester. You do 2x more work in terms of homework and exams, which brings it to ~150 hours. 3. Our comprehensive course, at Coding Interview Bootcamp, is 150+ hours. We do that within ~8 weeks, and we also include Systems Design. 4. The book, Elements of Programming Interviews, recommends ~150 problems in their most exhaustive scenario (#4, page 9). 5. Even Leetcode has ~150 problems in their most popular list. With those 5 observations, it empirically seems like you should set aside about 150 hours. Not supported by science, but with evidence. YMMV, because it really depends on where you start from.

Question: What are some examples of a good cover letter when applying to startups?

Online application systems receive SO MANY applications so fast that at the other end it’s rare for someone to find time to read your resume, much less your cover letter diligently. Even if they do, they just skim it and move on to focus more on the pedigree on your resume. And again, even if they do, they may not be the right person for the role you’re applying to (Applicant Tracking Systems are managed by recruiting teams, who are often far removed from hiring managers) and may not care to pass it on correctly. Gone are the days (permanently so), when, as a candidate, you’d look up job ads in newspapers/magazines, circle the mailing addresses, mail out paper resumes and also send something else along with, that explained to the company why/how/what-for that envelope has shown up at their doorsteps. That last paper was a cover letter. The now-relic used to go on top of the resume, to give more context. We have now lost that construct. And it won’t ever come back, at least in the developed world where the Internet is a thing. Spend that time writing a good resume (still matters) and a LinkedIn profile (so people can find you). And of course, spend time preparing for interviews. Having said the above, there are some reasons I can see where it may be useful to spend time writing such a letter: 1. Writing would give you clarity in your own mind, about how you want to position yourself and your subsequent verbal pitch. However, if you're going to do that well, then discussing with a knowledgeable coach is usually a much better way to go. 2. You are sending resume as an email attachment and want to say something in the email body. However, the email real estate is not very well suited to tell everything you’d want to say in a cover letter. 3. You have an entirely different, outstanding story/punchline to offer. However, if that is the case, then a cover letter isn’t sufficient or even necessary. That story needs to come out in many other ways. 4. You want someone else to forward your resume to a company, and that person doesn’t really know how to pitch you for the role. However, in this case, you’re better off talking with them first and then summarizing via email, to give them talking points. 5. You are just desperate and want to try everything you can, to land that role. You’re willing to take that infinitesimal chance that someone might click on that letter and whatever you have in there, will make a difference that nothing else will.

Question: How is finding the time complexity of an algorithm useful in the software field? If it is useful, how are industries implementing?
Answer: Getting into a habit of keeping time-complexities in mind when designing for solutions, is immensely useful in every-day software engineering. Let’s take a very very telling example: Imagine you are tasked with designing an updates feed. Something like Twitter’s feed or Facebook’s feed or Box’s updates’ feed: One way to start designing it, is to start thinking what are your sources of updates, then how to aggregate them, how to prioritize them, and how to display them. That’s classic, step-wise thinking by most engineers, who primarily don’t think in terms of time complexity. An engineer who primarily thinks in time-complexities, will first ask and answer this key question: How fast should the feed load? It must load in constant time O(1), otherwise someone with 10x more updates will have to wait for 10x longer. i.e. we need our updates pre-processed. i.e. we need a batch/offline process that aggregates updates and prioritizes them. Fast (how fast? Worst case linear time, of course!). And then we need an efficient querying mechanism that pulls them in constant time, by user. (how? Caching, of course!) Do you see the difference?

Question: I have heard I need to spend at least 1000 hours to prepare for the Google or Facebook interview. Is it true?
Answer: 1000 hours is too much. Let me explain, with some evidence. At Interview Kickstart, we’ve been doing this for a living. We’re in our 4th year and have trained nearly a thousand engineers to do well on challenging technical interviews, all across the planet. If you have a degree in CS and haven’t prepared for challenging DS/Algos interviews in a while, then it typically takes around 250 hours. Often much less. Only sometimes more. We observe, that when any learning is taking longer (not just learning for technical interviews), it is almost always because of some combination of one of the three reasons: 0. You are not doing it with the right mindset Many many people do DS/Algos problem-solving with the agonizing goal to crack into Google/Facebook. That’s often the wrong thing to do. You have to work on Ds/Algos problems with intrinsic motivation and enjoyment, transcending any possible ego and entitlement. Whether that prep leads to a job, is not in your hands. It’s a fool’s chase to connect the two. This is best explained by a one-minute impromptu advice by Bryan Cranston: (Don’t skip the video! It’s probably one of the most profound 1-minute video ever recorded) If you are not enjoying the problem-solving process, then it will take you much longer to reach the same goal. 1. Or You’re not following the right structure Even with the right mindset, you need something that tells you where to start and where to end, how to modularize, how deep to study, what parts matter and what don’t. You need to hear from someone who has done this before and gone over the hump. You need a forcing function on one hand, and one the other hand, you also need flexibility because you likely have a life outside DS/Algos also. These days, there are a plethora of websites and books, that, in some form, claim to give you a structure for preparation, but unfortunately don’t go far enough, or at all. If you get lost on one of those, then you’re just going to have to spend a ton of time wading your way through it. 2. Or You are not getting regular feedback Even with right mindset and right structure, it doesn’t work until you get periodic feedback. Whenever you’re learning something for a longer period of time, it is important to know how far you are. Otherwise it always feels like a bottomless pit. To give an analogy, think about how it feels when you’re driving to a destination, and you don’t know where you are currently. It gets agonizing, not to mention the potential to take the wrong exit and get lost, taking way more time than otherwise. You should hence do your mock interviews periodically. And/Or some practice interviews at companies you don’t care about. And/or programming contests. You should do something that pushes you to code in a fixed time and gives you a “judgment” at the end of it. Do enough of it, until such time that you are de-sensitized to getting judged. If all the three reasons above are taken care of properly, then you’re bound to finish your prep much sooner. Hit me up if you have follow-up questions: soham@interviewkickstart.com .

Question: Which tech company gives the hardest algorithm questions in interviews?
Answer: A question is never hard or easy. It’s the evaluation that is hard or easy. I have seen ICPC world finalists fail an interview when asked to reverse a string. And I’ve seen nascent bootcamp grads pass a Div-1 Topcoder interview with zero practice. It’s a lot up-to the expectation of the interviewer. A bit of luck too. Even if we put the interviewer aside, just the concept of easy or hard in itself is relative. What may need me to make multiple logical leaps (hard), may not be hard for you. Or vice-versa. Interviews are also not standardized processes. Even with a company, they differ a lot from panel to panel, interviewer to interviewer, time to time. Unless a company is small, even within itself, it’s difficult (if not impossible) to calibrate what is the hardest algorithmic question. Everyone will have their favorite and stories of how different candidates performed differently on their questions. Interviewers themselves learn better over time and calibrate their questions. A single technical interview is also more like a professional date, than it’s a test. A date is never hard or easy. An interviewer is not looking to see if the hard question is answered - s/he is looking to see if they can work with the person. And of course, there is nobody watching and calibrating all of this in aggregate. It’s very possible that hardest interviews once were given out by a specific panel in Google and they never met again. Or by a startup and they disbanded. etc. The closest anyone can get to a good answer that is independent of random personal experiences, is speaking in terms of averages of the masses: On an average, from aggregate experiences of most candidates, you’ll find hardest algorithmic questions being asked at Google. (I picked Google, because that is in aggregate we see from our vantage point. We have trained hundreds of software engineers who have interviewed at innumerable companies across the US, and in general, Google still comes up with more novel questions, and harder evaluations than others. In aggregate.)

Answer: Let’s break this down into two parts: How to overcome fear of DS/Algos and start practicing The answer here may be very counter-intuitive to some: The core idea to remove fear of anything, is to focus on creating a System, and forget about the Goal. Even if you doubt yourself, it will work. You’ll get better. One small concept to another. One insight to next. From here and from there. You will. You’ll then slowly ask for more complex problems. You certainly will. That’s just how learning works. That’s how every single human being is wired to do. Including yourself. So that’s how you get started. Make one simple, manageable system, and keep going back to it. You’ll automatically evolve from there. Question: Why are so many software engineering interviews just ridiculously and unnecessarily difficult (not just Google)?
Answer: That’s because those questions actually reflect the kind of work the company does. But you’re right - not all companies do that kind of work; only some do. Even at Google and Facebook, which are known of some of the most ground-breaking technical innovations in this generation, many many (most even) teams don’t do work that’s nearly as intellectually challenging as the interview questions they ask. So the real question is, why do they and some other companies, ask such questions for nearly all their software engineering roles? Following is the underlying corpus of reasons that compels most companies to do so: 1. Wherever possible, companies want to standardize the hiring bar across the entire department If companies don’t do that, then it can quickly get pretty chaotic. Some teams will feel superior to others and vice-versa. Internal mobility of engineers will become a lengthy and difficult process. They won’t be able to switch programming languages/stacks/tools that fluently. Each team will get a license to become a technical fiefdom, which will slow down the entire development process. Standardizing the hiring bar pre-solves for a number of problems in a short time. But then the question is, why standardize to challenging questions? 2. Without challenging questions, it’s slow and difficult to hire for many open positions in short time Most of these companies do such good work and pay so well, that they have a very strong pipeline of engineers applying to them. At Box, for example, it was routine to have hundreds of submissions for many open positions. If we threw easier questions in interviews, it would have rendered our entire tiered process useless (phone screens to onsites). After all, it is impossible to compare engineering capabilities of two engineers both of who can these days flawlessly reverse a string, and design a web-page with 3 buttons. (Granted, there are some companies who don’t have such strong pipelines, and/or are not hiring for so many positions and/or also not doing challenging work. Those companies should consider switching to a lighter interview process) But then the question is, how are so many engineers able to solve such problems? 3. Companies know, that candidates do targeted preparation for interviews, so the difficulty of questions has continued to inch higher Candidates have been preparing for technical interviews for 20+ years. First serious book (the most basic means of targeted preparation for anything) to come out and expose programming interviews was in year 2000. In last 17+ years, that landscape now has more seminal books, online judges, websites, sophisticated testing tools, ad-hoc meetups and even serious bootcamps[1] like ours. 4. Companies just want to have very driven engineers in all corners, and they can afford to Companies often only want to hire engineers who are capable of solving challenging problems, whether they actually have such problems on not. That’s because the belief is that the same engineers will often solve the mundane problems more innovative-ly and possibly at a different level of abstraction. They have to pay these gals and guys more, of course, because all competitors are vying for the same engineers. But that’s okay - they can afford it. They are either profitable like Google, or have easy access to VC money. At the end of the day, many of us just want to work with very driven people on whichever problems that are thrown at us. If a company can attract those people (like you and I!) and afford to pay them, then why won’t they do it? This apparently ridiculous and unnecessary process is working This process has been around for 30+ years largely in the same form (DS/Algos). Microsoft glorified it, then Google took the baton and now Facebook has carried it to yet another level. Many of these gals and guys at these companies are some of the most driven, most savvy and most impatient people on the planet. If something doesn’t work for them, they fix it in 30 minutes and don’t sit on it for 30+ years. But they haven’t even touched it. And they won’t. With a thousand foot pole. Because it works. You don’t like it? Guess what - your neighbor is willing to put up with it. Companies just want their problems solved. Doesn’t matter who solves them. If it’s not you, then it’s going to be someone else. I guarantee it.

Question: What might it be called in computer science where we have a tree structure where any given node can have 3 children (a left, middle and right child)? In my case, opening and closing tags, and then stuff that can go between/middle of those tags.
Answer: Are you looking for a Ternary Tree? Ternary tree - Wikipedia And of course, like John L. Miller suggested, in general, a tree with at most K nodes (children) at every node, is called a K-ary tree. A ternary tree is a special case of a K-ary tree. Before using a Ternary tree though, think hard if you actually need one. I obviously do not know your use-case, and whether it’s only academic, but I’ve often seen people tending to use a ternary structure when a binary would suffice. A common mistake is to create a third (or middle) node for something that can simply go as an attribute (value) of existing nodes.

Question: Is there life after a data structures course?
Answer: Nope. Not in this world anymore. But regret not - you will get reincarnated in a new world! Alphabetical lists will become sorted arrays to do a binary search. Never again, will you scan a list of names. It will be searched, one half at a time. If it is unsorted, then you will proudly take the high road and refuse to look up. A trip to a grocery store will be a quest for the shortest path. So will be finding a parking spot. And of course, only if the store manager knew of lookup tables, so that you won’t have to scan that entire damn isle for your favorite cereal. Pringles anyone? Pop one at a time from the stack, for it’s impossible to do it any other way. Back home, those pesky children are merely forks, really. Smalltime structures, not useful to handle real-world scale. Sometimes recursive. Why even play silly things like Jigsaw puzzles with them? Those are just backtracking problems. Even Sudoku. Don’t waste your time, lousy kids! Just write some loops and it solves itself. Ex calling? What? How can that be? We’re now such disjoint sets! Remember the fight we had when I argued that killing children is a perfectly normal thing to do? Yes, you just wait for them and if they don’t return, you just look them up by their IDs (who needs names?) and kill them. That’s what’s normal in CS. Standing in line for a movie ticket will also feel so normal. After all, it’s just FIFO. Though finding that the movie theatre is full will be a source of instant regret, for it is a lousy data-structure that can’t be dynamically resized! What agony. Back home again, trimming that tree is just an act of rebalancing. An upside down structure, that too. Did I tell you that backyards will merely become memory storage with pointers to trees? Hunting for an apartment? A graph problem, really. Thanks Dijkstra and every other person who already optimized it for me. Doesn’t really matter what apartment it is, as long as it’s found the most efficient way. Writing answers on Quora? Why do these muggles type paragraphs and paragraphs? Everything just needs to be a list. Then it can be traversed, instead of read. Welcome to the new world, a world where everything now is a quest for (data) structure and … simplicity :-) [Source: Years of training others in Data Structures and Algorithms for Challenging interviews: Interview Kickstart]

Question: How can I be a better programmer? I’m starting college and we need to learn Java. I’m feeling like I’m not good at all. I read the book, watch videos, and practice on CodeAcademy, but I’m not sure what else to do.
Answer: Thomas Alva Edison once said: “None of my inventions came by accident. I see a worthwhile need to be met and I make trial after trial until it comes. What it boils down to is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration.” Yes, you’re not inventing stuff at the pace Edison was. But from where you are, this is nothing short of an invention. Something totally new. Your perspiration looks correct, but if you feel that you’re still not succeeding, then one of the following is happening: If I were to teach you, I’d say you should start with a real need first. Something tangible, something that you can use in real life for someone e.g. your neighbor’s website, your barber’s app, or even your little sibling’s calculator. Something that is real and programmable in Java. As you go thru that project, you’ll have challenges to overcome. If you are interested in problem-solving (which is important to build a career in this field), you’ll naturally continue to address those challenges. You’ll learn, you’ll find people and resources that will help you and sooner or later, you’ll finish the job. All with Java, because that’s how you chose to do it. You may not write idiomatic Java, or the most perfect JavaDoc-strict Java, or with the most awesome design, but you will have solved a problem for someone. (which is what a programming language is ultimately supposed to do). It will take time, and it will take longer than what you think, but it’ll be worthwhile. Ideally you’d take this path under someone’s guidance, but it’s doable even without. If you’re not able to find a mentor, or you’re not able to overcome obstacles on your own, then that’s a strong indication that your heart is not in this (reason#1 above). But once you’re able to do this, it will inspire you. It will give you the right perspective to learn. It will help you shorten your learning curve, because you now know what is more important to learn. As you go down this path, you’ll start to see and use the power of Java to do more complex systems. The language, it’s ceremony, it’s efficiency and idiosyncrasies will pull you in more and more. More importantly, your successes with the language will feed your passion and you’ll never look back. God speed.
