Here is how: 20s is the first decade you’re operating independently of your parents. 20s is also the time, where you can and should invest in multiple things at once: 1. Your personal life Why 30 is not the new 20 This is a must-watch TED talk for 20-somethings. Clinical Psychologist Meg Jay makes a compelling argument: Contrary to the popular belief, 20s is not a throwaway decade. Just because marriage, work and kids happen later in life, it doesn’t mean you can’t start planning now. Invest in your personal life. Take the risk of falling in love, understanding people, breaking up when required and thus refining your understanding of your own self. 2. Your career “You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with.” — Jim Rohn Spend your 20s finding above-average people, people who are smarter and more driven than you. Then make yourself worthwhile, such that they let you into their circles. One straightforward way of doing that, is to go join a top company in your field. If you are a software engineer for example, go join Google or Facebook or several other strong technical teams. Most such top companies/teams will have a tough bar to entry. You’ll have to invest your time, energy and money into being worthy enough. Do that and do that until you succeed. 3. Your brain and mental health 20s are the final few years where your brain is continuing to develop: At What Age Is The Brain Fully Developed? Invest your time, money and energy into promoting a healthy brain development, and mental health at large. 4. Your physical health 20s is also the decade of highest physical energy in your life. Push yourself to do stronger workouts and longer travels. You’ll miss them later. In summary: 20s are possibly the most important decade of your lifetime. What happens or doesn’t happen in 20s, often has significant, irreversible bearing on your future life. Take whatever money you have and invest in building a better personal life, a stronger professional career, better mental health and stronger physical health. Sure, shove some of those savings into 401k, but in your 20s, the ROI on investing in yourself instead, is going to dwarf any 401k return by magnitudes.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why is ageism so rampant in the software industry?
Answer: Yes, ageism is real in software engineering, but whatever you do, don’t remove your age markers from your CV. You won’t be able to fight ageism by hiding your age. Take it head on. Hear me out. My experience in hiring/managing: I'm a 38 old software engineer. I've been lucky enough to be managing engineers from very early on. It started with managing research assistants on a small project with my professor in college, all the way to being a Director of Engineering at one of the fastest growing SaaS companies of all times (Box). I've hired and fired numerous engineers in my career - young guns, old ones and everyone in the middle, both men and women. And of course, I've evaluated numerous engineers by now, of all ages, all the way from resume screening to rejection after multiple on-sites. I'm not the only one in the world with this experience, but I'm at least one. And following are my thoughts/observations: Understanding ageism in general A. The problem of ageism is very natural, very human. It is human evolutionary survival tendency to prefer association with beings with perceived higher energy, who can also stay with us longer. We've all succumbed to it, subconsciously or otherwise, in some form. e.g. we rarely adopt an older dog from a shelter. We prefer puppies instead. We're just wired that way. This implies, that there is never going to be a blanket solution to this problem. Asking humans to go against evolutionary pressures, is practically impossible. Having said that, of all species, humans are the most patient and discerning beings, so they can consciously make a choice to not have that bias. But unfortunately very few people are internally consistent and strong enough to consciously ignore that bias. In order to make people ignore bias at scale (i.e. for entire teams and companies), the only way to make it happen in a democracy, is by setting cultural norms. That’s because cultural norms trump every other nuance of survival. B. Governments all over the world have been fighting against ageism. e.g. in the US, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) forbids age discrimination against people age 40 or older. Laws in other countries can be found here: INTERNATIONAL AGE DISCRIMINATION. Obviously it's very difficult to prove age-related discrimination, but the Governments do what they can. C. Ageism in interviews, is more rampant than ageism at work. In interviews, the company is more risk averse and benefit of doubt usually doesn't go to the candidate even as is. Age just makes it worse. But once you're hired, they try their best to find you your spot and have you there, as long as you keep performing. The laws also help you. D. It’s very difficult for a young person to realize what ageism truly means and truly understand the gravity of it. This, by definition, eliminates at least half the population (younger ones) in the working world who’d be able to empathize with you. Understanding ageism in Software Engineering A. Realize that ageism in software engineering is relatively new. That's simply because the field itself is relatively new. There are just not that many engineers over 40 yet. When I opted for Computer Science (CS) 20 years ago, tech was but one unpopular corner of the world, in the form of Microsoft, IBM and the likes. (It was viewed very much like we view Oil and Gas industry today i.e. a few companies in some corner). People in my generation hence often opted for branches like Mechanical, Civil, Medicine, Electronics, Chemicals and such, over CS. However, software engineering has exploded in last 20 years. Every company is now hiring software engineers and a lot more people have entered this field relatively recently. As a result, you see most teams have engineers that are still in their 20s, and 30s. And because young engineers don’t have to deal with ageism, there is still an absence of cultural norms around it. (see A above to relate). Going forward though, as more engineers age, you'll very likely see more discussion around ageism in software engineering, and cultural norms will emerge. B. Realize that ageism in software engineering has an early onset (compared to other fields). That’s because one gets outdated early in such a fast moving field. To remain relevant, it needs continual retraining, which many engineers are not able to do. C. Realize that software engineering is a field, where experience has little correlation to expertise. That’s also because the field changes so fast. How to deal with ageism in Software Engineering When it comes to finding a new job, software engineers can deal with ageism in a few different ways: A. Take it head on Definition of taking it head on, is that you still aim for a programming job that is equally/more challenging and pays more than your previous best, often top of market. When you find that job, you become a part of a younger team and keep up with them. The engineers who do this, believe that real problem is not ageism; real problem is that often engineers don't even try to keep up as they age. These heroes/heroines keep up their skills and energy to defy ageism in this fast moving field. Note that keeping up in our field is especially difficult to do. That’s because our field is unique: it's vast, there is a lot of competition (is very easy to get into), is not regulated and hence changes A LOT. e.g. There is NO other industry on the planet like this. If you think about refrigerators for example, the companies your parents bought refrigerators from, are pretty much the same as you will buy from, and your kids will too. Those are relatively slow moving industries. Keeping up with such an ever changing industry is hard. Very hard. It's tiring, expensive and never gives you a feeling of settling down. On top of that, the field pays decently well even to an average person, so there is little reason to push yourself and keep up. But if you want to remain well-paid software engineer in this field, you have to bite the bullet. And the most important thing in biting the bullet, is for yourself to not feel the burden of age. Older engineers often walk into an interaction feeling old instead of feeling upbeat. They often seek entitlement because of age, or rest on their laurels, instead of focusing on proving their skills again. Those who don't feel/do that, are the ones who are able to take this beast head on. e.g. We had hired two very senior engineers at Box, in their 50s and 60s. Those guys impressed the heck out of us in our interviews: Were they perfect? No. Were they faster than 20 years olds? No. But they gave us enough confidence that they will be valuable hires regardless. And they were. One of them recently retired after Box. Their secret? They had been like that from the get go. They always kept up. They kept changing jobs, kept learning new things, kept engaging with newer companies and newer audience. That internal drive to keep improving kept them young, as much as their grandkids did. Who brought them into interviews? Strong references. This is another thing that senior engineers have, and can do viz. connections. They actively build connections through their career, which helps them keep up and take the world head on. (Are you missing connections when sending out resumes?) B. Find a place where cultural norms support senior people There are at least three such places: One: Big companies. If you go to Google for example, there are many engineers in their 40s, and respecting seniority is in their cultural norms. e.g. If you are a senior engineer interviewing, they will put senior people in the interview panel. You can also go to Cisco, IBM, Oracle etc. They hang on to their senior engineers to maintain their large code-bases and don’t mind more of them. That's also a part of their cultural norms. Depending on which company you land, you may not get cutting-edge work or top of market compensation, but you'll still get decent work and compensation. If you want cutting-edge work as well as top of market comp, then you have to keep up your entire career. There is no escape. Two: Go to a place where there are fewer software companies and fewer engineers e.g mid-west US. Or e.g. internationally, where US experience is more valued. You may have to adjust to a different lifestyle, but that will afford you a longer and a more rewarding career in software engineering. Three: Start your own. You can then set your own norms. Your own consultancy or dev shop is a totally good idea. A lot of people start their own companies before ageism sets. This is a route I have taken. I set my own norms and I work with people I want to work with. C. Find a career where experience matters These could be adjacent careers like Product Management, People Management, Program Management, Project Management etc. In these careers people skills matter. Connections matter. Seniority matters. People believe you more when they see grey hair. So those careers gets better and more valuable with age. Best way to switch into these adjacent careers, is to do so inside your current company first. And then make a switch outside to graze in a better pasture. Alternatively one could switch to totally different careers e.g. Accounting or Medicine or Law, where more experience generally translates into higher performance and more value. Experienced doctors, lawyers and accountants can charge more. Not true for experienced software engineers. Switching to such totally different careers is practically impossible at a later age, but not unheard of. Whichever decision you make, it’d serve well to everyone to accept that ageism is real and as you age, you will need to make a conscious decision to deal with it in some way. Hope this helps? -Soham [InterviewKickstart.com]

Question: If there is such a high demand for tech positions, why don't they pay more?
Answer: You are kidding, right? Let’s try to see this from a more objective high level and paint some broad strokes: Take a look at this official source of US Govt data: Computer and Information Technology Occupations The median income for someone with an associate’s degree, is 66k+. Median income. i.e. half of income earners at that level, make more than 66k per year, just after 2 years of post-highschool education, if that. In order to ascend to higher levels of the pyramid, you need to remain up-to-date on newer, in-demand skills and target to work at some of the best tech companies. It’s amazing what a few months of preparation can do.

Question: What's a typical compensation package (salary, bonus, RSU) for an experienced software engineer with 5-7 years experience and a MS degree starting a new job at Google in LA?
Answer: At MS + 5–7 years of experience, at Google, you’re at the cusp of L3 and L4. Mostly L4, unless your interviews were a bit on the weaker side. L4 package at Google easily goes to $200K+ per annum (Cash + YearlyBonus + equity/4). Often more, with negotiations. We often negotiate Google offers for candidates from our programs. Here is what we have learnt: 1. Google DOES negotiate. It absolutely does. They routinely lose many engineers to up and coming startups (e.g. AirBnB,Uber and Snapchat), which has made them realize that they need to up their game. 2. Google mostly only negotiates with companies in the same tier. In order to move the needle at Google, you need to have competing offers. Good, competing offers from public companies, or pre-IPO companies. Think Facebook, Dropbox. 3. It depends a LOT on your recruiter. Some recruiters are very seasoned, and they play this psychological game very well. It’s very difficult to negotiate if you are caught with one of those. But other recruiters are more vulnerable. 4. Google CAN play evil. Yes, despite their motto. It’s rare, but it does happen. We once had an offer made at Level 3 for a candidate who was on the cusp of 3 and 4. The candidate declined, because they had other better offers (Uber, Dropbox) at higher levels. Despite having full knowledge of other competing offers, Google waited until the last minute, and only then offered Level 4, with the condition that the candidate sign the new offer as is, or they will be barred forever from interviewing with Google. Yep, it was a seasoned recruiter. In summary, if you have no competing offers from proper companies, and you really want Google, then you are pretty much at the mercy of your recruiter. They might move a bit if you persist and insist, but not much. In order to get something more meaningful out of them you need a strong competing offer. And a degree in psychology if your recruiter is seasoned.

Question: How do other senior software engineers prepare for coding interviews?
Answer: “Is this frustrating for others?” It surely is. But unfortunately there are no better ways to interview. Certainly not when a coveted company is hiring hundreds of developers at a time for a variety of positions. A process based on DS/Algos is still the most efficient process to interview at scale. Many many people have agonized and tried otherwise, but everyone, albeit frustratingly, has fallen back to this kind of process. See this more detailed treatise if you’re curious. “How did you approach it?” From what I see in my daily life: Roll up your sleeves and take it head on. Don’t wait for process to change; it won’t. If you want to work for one of these places that is. Realize that as an experienced engineer, your problem is not about knowing what to do - you know plenty about what to do, viz. which problems to do, which algorithms to do, which design questions to brush up etc. You also likely interviewed other people in your company. You were also not likely asked red-black tree verbatim (well, most companies don’t), but what you probably mean is you were asked something as silly, which can be learnt in a few hours prior, only if you knew. Your real problem, which you seem to be getting at, is how to find time/motivation to go thru all that shit again. Unlike last time in college, you now have many other pulls on your time viz. friends, family, hobbies, travel and maybe even kids. Here is another issue: After the “advent” of books and sites like Leetcode, Interview preparation for top-tier places, has been taking longer and longer for last 4–5 years. It used to be about one month affair part time. Now, it’s easily 3–4 months. Holding motivation for many months, when that’s not the primary thing in your life anymore, is hard and frustrating. But the options are even worse viz. stay where you are, or accept another mediocre offer. To tackle that, you need to impose a forcing function on yourself. Much like going to a gym, even though you very well know, that it’s eminently possible to stay fit even outside. But a gym is a gym. And a spinning class or a bootcamp in there, is even better. A periodic commitment to attend one of those, forces (read: motivates) you to do stuff, which you otherwise may not ever do. That group motivation done with the right people and continuous feedback, may just be the difference between living a diabetic all your life, and not.

Question: Why is Amazon’s hiring process so flaky and weird?
Answer: It’s not. Your expectations need to be different. Amazon in particular, is conglomerate like a bunch of startups within, instead of one cohesive team. And that’s true not just of Amazon. In our practice, we have witnessed intense variations in interviews of nearly every company. And that’s normal. Very very normal. That’s the nature of the beast and you can’t change the nature of a beast. A vast majority of people make the mistaken assumption, that interviews are like standardized tests (e.g. SAT, GRE, LSAT etc). Especially software engineers, where interviews rely a lot on algorithms and design skills. Interviews however, are more like a date than they are like a test. More precisely, they are like speed-dating. 4–5 first dates in rapid succession. In standardized tests, the evaluation is standardized i.e. one question has one acceptable answer. Whichever grader grades it, they will give you the same grade for a pair of question and answer. Not so in an interview. Same question and same answer can and often will be graded differently by different interviewers. That’s because interviewers are primarily there to ascertain whether you (the interviewee) match their beliefs and standards, and not whether you really know your red-black tree. Very much like a date. And everyone’s belief systems and standards are different. Similar but different. e.g. I may be okay if you use two {return } statements in your function, but I know interviewers who are not okay with that. If you interview with them, you’ll fail. Similarly, I have my own quirks (read beliefs, standards) when I take interviews. If you don’t match my beliefs, you aren’t going to get a good reading from me. What’s more, you yourself will also fall in the same boat, when you’re on the other side of the table. You’re going to bring your distinct self to the interview and not going to follow what your fellow interviewers do. Coming back to the point, following are all very normal: And many more variants. It all comes together in the roundup/debrief with the team/hiring committee and the decision is a complex web of those emotions and conversations. Not a standardized test at all, which gives the view of flakiness. So next time you’re in the interview room, make no mistake with your goal: your goal is not to get hired at Amazon. Your goal is to inspire the interviewer, to work with you. Perfectly answering a question is often a very necessary part of it, but not sufficient. You need to make that human connection too. Very much like making a sale, making a negotiation, a (professional) date. If it doesn’t go well, then very likely that wasn’t the right long-term relationship for you and that team. No hard feelings. Try another team/company. There are many many strong groups of people on this planet. Good luck!

Question: What happens to older (over 30) programmers? Do they get fired as they get older and "less innovative"? Does mid-career pay increase much for software engineers?
Answer: I'm a programmer in my late 30s, so hopefully I am "old enough" to answer this question :-) I have also hired older programmers in the past. First of all, realize that there just aren’t that many “old” (above 40) programmers. That is simply because programming (and computing tech in general), was not in such high demand 20+ years ago (I pick that time because kids opting for programming at/before that time would be 40+ today, which is the demographic we're wondering about). It is now that every taxi and toothbrush company needs programmers. Two decades ago, only "software" companies needed programmers and there weren't very many of those. Second, note that in the next five years, a LOT of programmers are going to hit 40. That is because many were introduced/converted into this field, during the tech boom of 1998–2000. So the real, first-hand answer to this question is going to come in next five-ish years, but here is my prediction on where you’re going to find them: 1. A lot of 40+ programmers are going to branch out of core programming, or they already have. First reason: Programming is not a regulated industry, like actuarial science or medicine or many others. The pace of innovation in this field hence, is staggeringly fast, and so is the pace of disruption of old technologies. Keeping pace with newer stuff constantly, is hard. Very hard. It’s easier to slide into adjacent areas, where programming experience is very valuable, but it doesn’t matter what language/tools/stack you have had experience in. e.g. People Management, Product Management, Program Management, Customer Support, Sales Engineering, Solutions Engineering, Systems Integration, Entrepreneurship, etc. Second reason: Many programmers went into programming because it was (and still is) a well-paying field, and not because they were suited for it. They know that it’s going to be difficult to sustain in an ever competitive market. 2. A lot of 40+ programmers will stay put in the bowels of big companies. A lot of “old tech” companies are hoarding experienced developers. Think IBM, Cisco etc. They have found their comfort zone there, and the companies also want to keep them, because they are original authors of the software that is sold. More importantly, companies know, that their older programmers are outdated, and not many places they can go to. So they can retain that older talent relatively cheaply. Sounds a bit evil, but it works out on both sides. So who is going to stay/survive in the field? The only ones who will continue to survive as core programmers, and command best salaries, are the ones These gals/guys have already had stellar resumes thru their 20s and 30s (e.g. open-source contributions, early engineers at successful tech companies), write code every day/week (much like writers write English), and more importantly, can’t fathom why they’d do anything else but programming. To all the young programmers there: 40s come at you very fast. Know yourself and your motivations clearly, and make your career choices wisely.

Question: What should I expect in a software engineer interview at Google, and how should I prepare?
Answer: 7 year old question, but still as relevant! Thanks for A2A Vincenzo Vicidomini. Google SE interview will depend on the level you are being interviewed at. Level-3 (or SE-II, there is no SE-I): This is the level where most entry level engineers are hired at, from BS or MS. There are 4 or 5 onsite rounds at this level. They are nearly all about coding of DS/Algos. For people on the cusp of L3 and L4 (below), they may throw in a design question, but usually not. Level-4 (or SE-III): This is for candidates with BS + 8 years, MS + 5 years, PhD + 2 years. Approximately. At this level, expect 4 or 5 onsite rounds also, but certainly at least one Systems Design question. Level-5 (or Senior SE) This is where many experienced engineers get hired. At this level, expect the same 4 or 5 onsite rounds, and two Systems Design questions. Level-6 (Staff Engineer) Level-7 (Senior Staff Engineer) Level-8 (Principal Engineer) Direct Hiring at levels 6, 7 and 8 is much rarer/harder than hiring 3 through 5. Here, the interview process, besides coding and design, also has a component of the domain you are coming in from. It is rare to get hired at Staff and Principal directly at many other companies, not just Google. Several reasons for that, which are out of scope of discussion here. Level-9 (Distinguished Engineer) Level-10 (Google Fellow) Nearly impossible to be hired directly here. Jeff Dean (Senior Google Fellow, added 2013) Enough said. About preparation The bar for clearing SE interviews these days, has gone up considerably compared to when this question was asked. Preparation these days takes at least 3 months for most candidates, especially if you have never had a rigorous course on DS/Algos in your college or elsewhere. There are many ways to prepare e.g. There are websites, there are books and there are courses. If you are a CS student in college, then the best way is to form a study group in school, and do online prep, like Leetcode. You’re targeting Level3, so you won’t need Systems Design stuff. If you are a working professional, then your biggest problem is motivation and carving out the time to prepare. I’d highly recommend taking a course for it. Much like going to a gym. A course has many other benefits e.g. being taught by engineers who have done hundreds of interviews at G, or getting continuous feedback, or having a motivated group of peers, or guidance on offer negotiations etc. Click here to get to know us better: Coding Interview Preparation Bootcamp, Large Scale Systems Design Interview Preparation Bootcamp

Question: How do I prepare to answer design questions in a technical interview?
Answer: Short answer: Take a structured, rigorous, course for it. When it comes to interviewing at your favorite companies, stakes are too high and such opportunities too few. Longer answer: In today's open and connected world, it's relatively easy to find good material on anything new you want to learn, whether it's cooking or systems design, or data-science. You can see pointers in many excellent answers here and elsewhere. All it takes is a google search for anyone, including your competition. But when it comes to finding opportunities at top-tier companies, most candidates need competitive advantage. Your competitive advantage in today's world is not in finding the best available material. It is in how fast and effectively you understand the material, how deep you go, what kind of feedback you get, and how you validate what is enough, and whether you’re there. That's where a structured course really helps. Learning with someone who has done this stuff many times before, in company of talented peers, shortens your learning curve by a magnitude. You make less rookie-mistakes and are ready faster for a better role. Of course, even better than taking a course, is to build those systems yourselves, especially at work if you can. But most tech companies on the planet are not solving scaling problems. As a software engineer working at such places, one doesn’t get to learn much of that on the job. Yes, one can build something on the side, but there is little real-life validation there. e.g. You could simulate high traffic using any number of load tools out there, but those will never surface the bottlenecks that real traffic will. Short of that, for such high-stakes interviews, I strongly believe, that your best option has to be, to take a structured, rigorous, interactive, time-bound and accountable course for it. Again - the question is never whether you are able to learn something new on your own by reading stuff from Internet. Question is always whether you can do it better than your competition. Often, just a tad bit of competitive advantage is all it takes to leap from a mediocre company to a great one. Question: What percentage of software engineers that have already been matched to a team make it through the Google hiring committee?
Answer: It looks like Google has recently been experimenting with its hiring process, at least when it comes to experienced software engineering positions. Earlier, all candidates had to be blessed by the Hiring Committee (HC) before the team matching phase. Now, for many candidates, they have switched the order of these two steps. i.e. Given your interview performance and profile, they first see if there is enough interest from a team at Google, and only with that blessing, the recruiter takes the profile to the HC. If no team at Google wants to take a chance on the candidate, then the profile may be forwarded to HC as is, but then the chances of them getting thru HC are less, despite a good interview. Exactly how long a recruiter waits for team matching to happen before conceding, is largely driven by how long the candidate can wait, and what’s reasonable. We’ve seen people wait up-to 3 months, and we’ve seen immediate matches also. If some team at Google wants to take a chance, then the HC takes that into serious consideration when reviewing interview feedback and delivering the verdict. Exactly why and how the process change has been implemented, when did it start, and for how many, is not something that’s possible to know/guess from outside.

Question: Why are reports still an important part of programming?
Answer: Yes, because reports facilitate fast business decisions. And a software engineer works for the business first, and for platforms/languages second. In an ideal world, there would be real-time reports, such that a decision-maker can click and get upto-the-minute reporting. But the world isn’t ideal, and a lot of data still flows manually between systems. That makes it inevitable to have someone write a program to generate custom reports. On the flip side -with the advent of modern HR and Analytics systems, this task of making custom reports is also reducing over time. i.e. while we many still need people to run reports for decision makers, more and more systems will continually get better at reporting and analytics, and we won’t need as many programmers to generate reports.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why do tech companies base interviews on coding and algorithm questions where interviewees who have seen the question will obviously do better?
Answer: Let’s split this into two: 1. Why ask coding/algorithms questions at all? They are not even related to work! A lot has been written about this. See this Quora answer for one deep perspective. In brief, the currently pervasive culture of coding and algorithms questions in interviews exists, not because it’s the best way to interview, but because it’s the most convenient way to interview. That’s true especially at scale, where a company is hiring 10s (e.g. Box) or 100s (e.g. Uber) or 1000s (e.g. Google) of engineers a quarter. 2. Why ask cliche questions that someone with preparation can do better with? * It’s very difficult to come up with good, new technical interview questions. Takes hours, if not days, to come up with a proper question, which can be solved in 30–45 minutes within an interview setting. We see new questions mostly only come up from big companies, and that too mostly G and F. Interviewers at nearly all other companies reuse questions they have recently seen. So much easier than divining and testing a new question on your own. * If you don’t prepare, then you may fumble for a long time, and lead the interviewer to frustration As an interviewer, 8 out of 10 candidates you meet, are not able to solve even the most basic problems. After a while, that starts to negatively weigh on you, and interview become a boring burden. And you want to quit interviewing. Instead, I’d much rather have a conversation with you after you are prepared, instead of before. I don’t want to waste my time seeing you fumble on simple things. Still, 8 out of 10 people do, and it’s super frustrating to sit there watch you struggle for 30 minutes. So if not for anything else, then just my sanity, I’d like you to prepare and have a quality conversation with me. e.g. if I ask you to traverse a directory tree to look for duplicate files, it is extremely frustrating to see you stumble with tree navigation. I’d much rather have you discuss the strategies of traversals (DFS vs BFS, Stack vs Recusion) etc, and debate those with the use-case in mind, instead of trying to divine one on your feet (or give up). * If we don’t allow and expect preparation, then we are saying that we believe in talent over prep, which is false. I believe in inherent talent/ability, but only when it comes to being the best of the best. But interviews are not looking for best-of-the-best. Interviews are only looking for good engineers, and being a better engineer is doable with preparation. I want to give you an opportunity to prepare before coming, and my hope is that the right kind of prep will lead you to be a better engineer. If I see that you are well-prepared in an interview, then I’ll take you deeper into the problem, discuss pros and cons of solutions available and/or generally get to know you better as a person. That would give me a much stronger signal of you. On the flip side, even after preparation, if I find you lacking, then that gives both of us a lot more confidence in rejection.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: How much does software engineering interview preparation actually help?
Answer: This question hits home. From my experience, here is the answer => (1) Almost anyone can get a job at Google if they practice enough for the interviews. Let me explain. Interview prep doesn’t get you into “Google”; being a good engineer does! Very first thing to realize, is that our premise (viz. that practicing for interviews gets you into “Google”), however popular, is fundamentally flawed. That’s not how it works. What gets you into “Google”, is you being a good engineer first; not just being a good interviewee. Experienced interviewers, especially at good companies, can very easily tell the difference. The right goal for interview preparation hence, is to be a better engineer, and not to get a job at “Google”. The thing to realize, is that, when you put yourself thru a preparation regime that has interview-type constraints and challenges, that improves you faster than any casual method. That is a little-known fact, that now you know :-) What kind of preparation makes you a better engineer? Here are the characteristics of the right kind of preparation: 0. Preparation done with a clear understanding of today’s unique opportunity We currently live in a time where due to the demand-supply skew, software engineers make at par small-business owners, medical doctors and investment bankers, often starting very early in their career. That’s not true of all software engineers though. It’s only true for those who have taken the pain to better themselves in their craft. If you don’t approach your preparation with this overall backdrop of context, then you won’t go very far. Eventually, you’ll regret not having tried enough, and spending your career with mediocre companies, even when there was a clear path to better teams. 1. Preparation with primary focus on solving problems, instead of getting a job I’ve cited this video elsewhere before. I’m going to cite this again, because it’s just so powerful. And Bryan Cranston says this better than anyone else I’ve seen: 2. Preparation where you are holding your discipline through struggle One kind of struggle is struggle for survival, to make ends meet e.g. “find any job”. The other kind of struggle for something higher viz. something you don’t really need it to survive e.g. “find a job at Google”. The latter kind of struggle is often harder to sustain. If you shy away from it, then you will slip into mediocrity. In other words, even if you are making a salary that’s enough for your family to survive and build a nest-egg, if you want to work with the the most driven technical teams of like-minded people, you need to buckle up and keep getting better as an engineer, to get into “Google”. 3. Preparation where there is ample and continuous feedback Feedback is the only thing that leads to improvement. Feedback has to be specific kind too. It’s one thing to have just test-cases of a problem pass online, but it’s entirely another thing to make sure that your coding is fluent, code is efficient and that it’s expressed properly in a conversation. It is hence important to seek feedback in various ways e.g. timed tests, mocks interviews etc. It is also important to seek frequent feedback, in order to maintain a certain level of continuity in calibration. You don’t need to be Jeff Dean to crack into “Google” Becoming best of the best is probably limited by inherent talent, but being just great or good enough is certainly not. And one doesn’t need to be world’s best to crack into “Google”. It’s sufficient to be a generally good engineer, which is doable with the right practice. If you are preparing with the right mindset, and sustaining your discipline for the required time with continuous feedback, then there is no way in hell you won’t get better as an engineer and thus get a seat at that coveted table. Question: How do the technical leader/manager and software engineer interview processes differ in the top tech companies?
Answer: Short answer: Depends on the company. Just ask the recruiter. It’s not very sensitive information; they will tell you enough. Long answer: Really, just depends on the role, company culture, and what the leadership believes. There are well-understood patterns, but no written rules. If you are not interviewing for a pure people manager position (e.g. if you are interviewing for a classic TL/M role), then you’re still considered very much an individual contributor (IC). Nearly all of your interview will resemble a Sr. IC interview. You will have one or two soft-skills interview, but not more. It’s also relatively rare for a company to hire TL/Ms from outside. TL/Ms are also mostly promoted from within, because that’s an excellent way to reward a high performer. And yes, after your interview, your level is determined e.g. SDE 2, 3, Staff etc. Even there, some companies have different ways of slotting, plus it depends on how well you negotiate that. It gets more nuanced if you’re interviewing for pure people-managerial roles: Some companies believe, that a people manager should be at least as good as a senior engineer in technical skills. Not necessarily in fast algorithmic coding, but in design skills, in code reviews, and in technical probing. Otherwise it’s difficult to get the respect from engineers reporting into them. Such companies will usually have two groups of interviews. In one, they’ll check the candidate’s technical knowledge and in the other one, they’ll probe their soft skills. Some companies OTOH, don’t care. They believe that a people-managerial role, even in a core technical org, is mostly about prioritizing and influencing. For technical stuff, they can be paired with a strong technical person. Such companies will dive deep into your soft skills (sometimes so much so, that you’d wish they checked for technical skills instead :-)).

Question: What does Balaji Viswanathan think about Donald trump's H1B visa bill? How could it effect the IT sector in India and is it preferable to pursue MS in USA after this bill?
Answer: Would love for Dr. Balaji Viswanathan (பாலாஜி விஸ்வநாதன்) to answer this. Meanwhile a similar question was answered on Quora here. I’ll paste my answer from there: tl;dr: If it passes the way it is worded, the bill will reduce the pool of available visas to Indian IT firms. But 130K is not the minimum wage those clickbait headlines make it to say; that’s something different. Let me explain First, some background: 1. Indian IT firms are very large users of H1B In fact, some would say, that they are the biggest users. e.g. see here: Indians got 86% of the H1B visas for tech firms issued by the US in 2014 - The American Bazaar 2. There is wide-spread myth in the US about “H1B workers taking jobs” from Americans Jobs are outsourced due to cost-savings of globalization, not due to H1B. For every IT worker Indian companies bring to US, there are 10 that are back in India, doing the work. Sponsoring H1B visas is also expensive viz. $8–10K, and the whole point of outsourcing is not to increase costs. It’s hence in the interest of IT companies to bring as few workers as possible. But there is just so much work outsourced and massive cost savings thereof. Yes, some American workers do lose their jobs, but it’s because of reduced costs due to globalization, and not because of H1B. e.g. if a company outsources 100-workers’ worth work to India, the work of 80 of those 100 workers will now be done offshore, and not in US. Only about 20 workers’ worth of work will be done locally, which may be displaced by H1B workers. Also, note that most of those 100 jobs, are relatively low-skilled jobs. Do you really think a company is going to outsource their most important jobs to overseas people? However, whenever even few jobs are lost, it gets a lot of bad press and complains to the lawmakers’ offices. A little too much of it. That is what prompts legislators to bring these reform acts. After all, they also want to feel relevant, like all of us are. Now let’s analyze the bill in some detail Here is the current wording of the bill, for the curious, patient and frustrated: https://lofgren.house.gov/upload... At first, I was shocked, when I read that “minimum is 130K” headlines. But when I dug into it more, I realize that 130K is not what it means. H1B dependent employers are employers with at least 15% workers that are H1B dependent. Turns out, most Indian IT firms are not H1B dependent employers. See here: H-1B-dependent employer - Wikipedia . There are intricate ways of calculating and attesting that, and the bill doesn’t address any of that. [Edit: A couple of readers pointed out, that many Indian IT firms are indeed classified as H1B dependent. For this, a more reliable source than Wikipedia is: Solution for Work Visa, Student Visa, Visa Jobs and Green Card . Note though, there too, you will still find some LCA applications from the same employers, which are filed indicating no H1B dependency. That may be a mistake on their part] It simply means, that if you don’t want to pay that much, you have to fill out some extra paperwork viz. “attestations” that you won’t do such and such things. All those “things” to be attested/promised are very fluffy and difficult to prove. And have been around since the 90s. This bill doesn’t address any of that. Language includes doing a “market based compensation”, including “cash bonus” and “other similar compensation”. It’s anyone’s guess how this can be gamed. This bill doesn’t pay attention to that. In other words, no “130K” isn’t too relevant to Indian IT firms. What may affect the Indian IT firms The thing that may affect IT companies, is the intent of the bill to do “market based” allocation. e.g. if some employer is willing to pay 200% of wage, they will get a preference in allocation. In order to reduce costs, IT firms will very likely not pay very high salaries to H1B workers they bring here, and thus may lose those visa applications to other employers willing to pay higher. Reservation of 20% of quota for small employers will also reduce the pool of available visas for these big firms. Plus, the minimum wage tier has also been removed, which will increase costs for the IT firms. However, writing was on the wall for a number of years and these firms have already anticipated this tightening. They have hence moved a lot of their visa allocation to L1 visas. The bill doesn’t address the real issue The way it is, falls short in a number of ways in addressing real problems. Apart from the ones I mentioned earlier, the other real issue, is the power imbalance between the employer and the employee. The employer has just so much influence on the job and say on the career of the employee, that you can easily find H1B employees stuck working for same employers for years together, with low salaries. The other thing influencing condition of H1B workers, is the one following and bigger mess viz. Green Cards, which has ridiculousness of its own. That is also not addressed by this bill. Finally, there are multiple such bills So this is not the only H1B reform bill. While this is the most jazzy of all reform bills bill, there are multiple bills. We don’t know which bill will be discussed/enacted. If you are in the US or planning to come to US, your best bet is to work for some of the top employers. e.g. Google, Facebook, etc, who have offices all around the world. Work hard to get in there, get treated fairly, get paid very well, and make an amazing career without worrying about this political mess.

Question: What kind of software engineers will always be employed, even during market crashes?
Answer: Having coached hundreds of working professionals, I’ll claim that your assertion is flawed. This: “being so good that the instant you're dissatisfied with your job, another top company will welcome you with open arms”, is a very deeply perpetrated myth. Being good at anything is very very context sensitive. It’s not possible to be good in isolation, and your being good at anything is very dependent on the kind of support system you receive (professional support from your team, or family support, direct or indirect). Not to mention your age and business domain. If you have found your groove at one company, or in one project, there is nothing to say, that you’ll find it again in the next place with the same fervor. I have lots of stories of people who stay at one place for a while, do well, and then bounce around for a while, looking for a home again. I’m not saying you shouldn’t pay attention to your skills, but if you are optimizing for having a job all the time, then for a second, I’d urge you to keep that notion of being “so good” aside and look at some other things that may matter more during a downturn: The engineers who will always have a job when the market crashes, are the following: And finally, here is the kicker: I don’t think you should optimize for having a job always. In other words, you should optimize for the upside, not to protect the downside. Protecting for the downside is an entirely different skill, with an entirely different set of constraints. It’s an energy sink, and most of it has nothing to do with being good at your technical skills, except maybe interview preparation ;-). - Soham Coding Interview Preparation Bootcamp

Question: Why do interviewers care so much about algorithm and data structures?
Answer: [Image Courtesy: ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ on Twitter ] For fresh grads, part of your hunch is correct. Because of their lack of production-quality experience, we don’t ask too many language/tool/stack/technology specific questions in technical interviews. And when we do, we don’t expect them to know the nuances like a practitioner would do. But that expected lack of experience with specific tools, is not the reason we ask DS/Algos questions in technical interviews. We ask DS/Algos questions also to experienced engineers. Yes, DS/Algos are rarely coded directly in your daily work - in fact, we categorically know that you’re unlikely to use many of them directly, if ever, in your entire career. In fact, if I simply want you to sort a dataset at work, I’d categorically expect you to not code Quicksort in 30 minutes. I’d instead expect you to start with SQL or Command line, and I’ll give time for you to learn it, if you don’t already know it. But, knowing all that fully well, we still ask DS/Algos questions in interviews. That is because technical interviews follow a very different set of constraints and allowances, when compared to actual work. While no interview questions are perfect (much less DS/Algos) and no single type of questions are ever used in isolation, asking DS/Algos questions has numerous advantages to the company, and has important advantages to the candidates (e.g. they let you switch your domain). Following is a relatively long multi-part treatise, explaining this approach. This has been received very well by hundreds of candidates from the course as well as my other speaking engagements. If you have not thought about this before, you may find several useful insights at inconspicuous places below. I hope that it’ll be an interesting read, and worth your time. First of all, pat yourself on the back for asking this question. So many engineers agonize about DS/Algos in interviews, but never once stop to ask this question: why is it such a central part of interviews nowadays? Just trying to answer this question puts you miles ahead of competition. Due to my profession, I breathe technical interviewing. I’ve been asked these questions in my interviews, I have myself asked DS/Algos questions as a hiring manager at Box and before, I’ve helped tech companies set detailed interview processes, I’ve helped head-hunters screen candidates and I’ve also helped candidates do well in such a process. —— 0. The precursor The precursor to DS/Algos types questions, as you may already know, are puzzles and brain-teasers. Puzzles have long been a part of “tradition of tech interviewing”, if I may call it so. A really good introduction to this history, is found in the seminal book How would you move mount Fuji?. Quoting from pages 6 and 7 of that book: “Logic puzzles, riddles, hypothetical questions, and trick questions have a long tradition in computer-industry interviews. This is an expression of the start-up mentality in which every employee is expected to be a highly logical and motivated innovator, working seventy-hour weeks if need be to ship a product. It reflects the belief that the high-technology industries are different from the old economy: less stable, less certain, faster changing. The high-technology employee must be able to question assumptions and see things from novel perspectives. Puzzles and riddles (so the argument goes) test that ability.” —- While that sheds some light on what the origin was, it still leaves the picture incomplete. At least to me. There need to be some distinct advantages to the process, for it to be so prevalent. And there are. I’ll try and enumerate those below, wearing my Hiring Manager (VP Engineering) hat: 1. They fit the best known method of interviewing, very well Interviews, by definition, are supposed to be a predictor of future performance at work. But humans are not that simple. Same person behaves differently in different contexts at different times, rendering most predictions useless. In fact, being “predictable” goes against the most fundamental evolutionary goal of survival. Humans wanted to remain unpredictable, so that they won’t be hunted down. For a long time now, it has been known, that interviews in general, in any field, are a poor predictor of future job performance. See some pointers to that research here: Should we stop interviewing people? Here is some more reinforcement of that, from the horse’s mouth: Google’s SVP of HR talking about their interviewing: Even Google Doesn't Do Interviews Better “We looked at tens of thousands of interviews, and everyone who had done the interviews and what they scored the candidate, and how that person ultimately performed in their job. We found zero relationship. It’s a complete random mess…” So what do we do? Can we stop interviewing and start hiring randomly? No, we cannot, because however sub-optimal the act is, it at least gives us, the hiring managers, a mental satisfaction of trying our best. Trying hence is the keyword. In that spirit, the question really is - what is the best we can do? In other words, what do I test in an interview, such that it gives me the highest possible confidence in predicting your future performance? To answer that question, here is the most relevant and comprehensive meta-research: http://mavweb.mnsu.edu/howard/Schmidt%20and%20Hunter%201998%20Validity%20and%20Utility%20Psychological%20Bulletin.pdf “This article summarizes the practical and theoretical implications of 85 years of research in personnel selection. On the basis of meta-analytic findings, this article presents the validity of 19 selection procedures for predicting job performance and training performance and the validity of paired combinations of general mental ability (GMA) and the 18 other selection procedures. Overall, the 3 combinations with the highest multivariate validity and utility for job performance were GMA plus a work sample test (mean validity of .63), GMA plus an integrity test (mean validity of .65), and GMA plus a structured interview (mean validity of .63). “ In other words, if I don’t ask you some challenging questions (testing GMA), and make sure you also know how to write code (Work Sample), in a structured manner, then my interview of you is merely a coin-toss. DS/Algos questions fit that bill nicely. They can be constructed to be as challenging or as easy as required, to get a good read on your preparation. They can be evaluated more objectively, and they also show your abilities of what you’re going to do at work (write code). If we compare those with other types of questions, the fitment becomes more clear: e.g. Knowledge-based questions (e.g. Java), while can be argued as work-sample tests, they don’t really test the GMA, and are difficult at best to make new/challenging. Also, Software engineering is not a knowledge-based role - it’s a problem-solving role. if companies want to hire knowledge-based roles, they generally just hire contractors. IQ tests are difficult to administer and are not socially acceptable. Heck, even puzzles and riddles are going away from social acceptability. Questions on your past experience are necessary to ask, but not sufficient and like we noticed in the research, they are not a good predictor of future performance. Questions on designing systems similar to what you’re going to design at work, are a close second, and we use them a lot too, but it’s very tedious to get enough variety in them. Plus they are subjective as hell. Note, that as a candidate too, you want to fit into the company, as much as the company wants you to fit in. So you want the company to pick the best possible method of evaluating your candidacy. —— 2. They make it very convenient for companies to interview at scale . Very. When it comes to most good tech companies, you have to realize a couple of things: First: They are not just interviewing. They are interviewing at scale. They are flushed with resumes to the tune of hundreds a day. Second: Interviewing is not anyone’s favorite thing. Spending time on interviewing is the last thought ever. Most engineers don’t ever want to spend time in interviewing. Most of the attention and time at work, is spent in building features and products and shipping them out the door. Interviewing is a necessary evil, at best. There is an entire department for Hiring, but not for interviewing. They are not the same thing. Yes, there are people and pockets who will tell you otherwise. But the moment it comes to getting their bonuses, it’ll be on how many features shipped, not how many engineers interviewed. Maybe in one or two quarters of crunch, the department will encourage more interviewing, but you’re kidding yourselves if you think they are giving it more attention than absolutely minimally necessary. Regardless of their lip-service. Turns out, DS/Algos questions are a boon to companies, when it comes to scaling an interview process with minimal time spent. Let’s see how: * It’s very easy to train the interviewers on them In fact, no formal training is necessary. Pick up any random book or website, read the question, read the answer and deliver it. Also, interviewers only need to get good at just a few questions, maybe 2 to 5. Then they can interview for months together, without knowing or getting good at anything outside that comfort zone. Not fair, you say? Of course, but fairness is not the goal. Goal is to spend least amount of time, not to prove whether it’s fair or not. * They make it easy to evaluate and compare candidates quickly The answers are so closed ended, that it doesn’t need a long debate to tell which candidate did better on reversing a string. And remember, if both candidates don’t cut it, then there are new candidates all the time! * They make it easy to standardize and centralize the process Now you’re not limited to engineers from a certain team to interview members of that team. Whoever is available, can come and do the interview. You can also do rotations of interviewers, so that a select few are not burdened. And of course, you can just create a question bank, so others can pick from there. Not fair you say? Yep, not the goal. See above. —— 3. DS/Algos questions afford great flexibility in the interview room When it’s 1x1 time, they have distinct advantages: * They can be made arbitrarily easy or arbitrarily hard. On the fly Candidate not doing well? Dumb it down to make them feel better. Candidate doing very well? Keep throwing constraints and making it more challenging. Want to get more collaborative with the candidate? DS/Algos questions can be easily morphed into those too! * They can be administered in any writing mode Whiteboarding? Check. Want to write on a piece of paper? Check? Use your own computer? Check? Use an online IDE? Check. Take home exams? Check. These questions are small enough that they can be very flexibly delivered by the company, in any mode you like. * They are agnostic to candidate’s past Isn’t it amazing when you can free the candidate from their past and just have them showcase their skills? Schools, pedigree - why should all that matter? * They avoid storytellers, lets companies hire problem-solvers There is no time for story-telling in a DS/Algos interview. Either you can think and code, or you cannot. It’s that clear. * They can bring out candidate’s behavior when challenged This is subtle, and often overlooked. But when I challenge a candidate on something hard, whether they succeed or not, but how they handle that tells a lot about them. Do they take hints when I give them? Are they respectful? Is their head firmly in solving the problem, or do they get distracted? Do they give up? Those are immensely valuable traits to know, which don’t come out any other way. —- 4. They are candidate friendly! Don’t believe me? For candidates, here are some invaluable advantages in this approach: * They let you switch your technical domain! Right? If you are coming from X domain and I want you for Y, how else will I know, that you’re a good software engineer? As an interviewer, I know nothing about your domain, and you know nothing about mine. Where the hell do we meet? DS/Algos questions provide that lowest common denominator. Otherwise if you worked in Payment systems in your first job, you’ll hole yourselves to that, all your programming career. * Now you’re not stuck to your programming language! If you are a Java programmer, you can continue to interview in Java, even though my shop may be doing PHP. I understand, that good engineers rise above languages, and this lets you have that chance to write code in something you know well. Otherwise, good luck switching to a new stack, ever! * You can truly prepare for technical interviews! YES! Companies scream at the top of their voices, for you to not come to the interviews without preparation. They send you prep material, recommend books and courses! They are not stupid! Go back to reason #2. Interviews are not their favorite thing to do and suck a lot of time out of more important things. As an interviewer, I’d much rather compare two prepared candidates, than suffer thru an ill-prepared candidate. That’s because I know what I’m looking for - your preparation is not going to cloud my judgment in an incorrect way. I understand, that it’s up to me, and I want you to prepare, so as to respect my time in the interview. e.g. If I ask you a Graphs question and you fumble thru a BFS/DFS implementation, there is nothing more frustrating and boring than that. I’d much rather see you fly thru it, and then discuss tradeoffs of different solutions. —- 5. Downsides of this process are not that big for anyone Following are some downsides to having DS/Algos questions in the interview process. But notice that none of these are unique to these questions, or wild. They are relatively easy to address: * Downside: Interviewers still have to know what to look for Asking DS/Algos questions can quickly devolve into a game of finding the best answer. But that’s not the right thing to look for. Right thing to do, is to pay attention to the thought process (more on this in a different answer). This however, does come around with experience. Once you do a few interviews, you’ll naturally calibrate yourself to look for what matters. * Downside: Candidate performance on these questions is equally dependent on interviewERs In other words, if you take someone thru a set of 5 engineers in a company, there is no guarantee that they will do well with another 5 people in the same company. Another way of saying this, is that beyond a certain preparation level, your interview depends on the interviewERs as much as it depends on your preparation. That sucks for candidates, but it’s OKAY for companies, because they have enough information to call your candidacy, with whichever set of people interviews you. If you clear one panel, then they will find sufficient documentable reason (read: excuse) to hire you. And remember, they have to hire. So they won’t put you thru another ringer! * Downside: Lots of false negatives There are many candidates who don’t know about the process, or who fail to prepare, or who just outright reject to be subjected to these. Among those, there are many good candidates (false negatives) that the company is losing. But you know what, companies don’t care much about losing false negatives, because they have a steady supply of people who are happy preparing for and going thru this process! Also note that none of these downsides are unique to DS/Algos based interview process. In fact, there is no perfect interview process. For candidates, the only “downside” is that they have to prepare. That can be annoying, but when done right, it can be very very enjoyable, and you’ll learn a lot. We know that, because many candidates come to the course with no intent to even look for a job. That, according to my subjective belief, is the hallmark of a good course. —- 6. When not to use DS/Algos questions This section is strictly not a reason per se, but the reasoning is not complete without understanding when we shouldn’t use them. * Don’t use them when you’re not interviewing at scale Hiring for only 1 or 2 positions a quarter? Don’t have a pipeline like the hot tech companies do? Rethink your process. You have time to pay attention to build a more tailor-made process for your role and the type of person you’re seeking. Don’t just blindly emulate the top places. * Don’t use them for candidates whose reputation precedes them If the candidate has something to show for e.g. a popular open-source project that you’re trying to hire for, try to get a better idea of their current skills by doing some design questions with them. * Don’t use them on candidates with direct domain experience Once in a while, you see a candidate who has done exactly what you want them to do in the team. If you can reasonably say, that you will want that role for the foreseeable future to stay as is, then structure the interview very precisely to that domain. * Don’t use them, if you don’t appreciate them, or understand them I’ve been told of many instances when the interviewers have delivered questions despite not knowing how to solve it themselves. That’s just evil and incompetent. Don’t ever do that. You’ll not inspire good people to join you if you do that. I hope I can make you see, that while DS/Algos questions are not the best or only question-type used in technical interviews, in grand scheme of things, they are the most convenient from multiple perspectives, and hence have found their groove. Convenience - Isn’t that how life works most of the time anyway? :-) - Soham Coding Interview Preparation Bootcamp

Question: I recently graduated with a degree in CS. Why won't anyone give me six figures during negotiation?
Answer: It’s simple: Because in company’s perception, there were other people (CS grads or not), who could do the same job for less, and with the same quality. Businesses don’t pay for your CS degree - they pay to get their work done. But it can be complicated: I don’t know any particulars about our situation, and obviously it’s very difficult to know the precise reason. But having been a part of numerous salary negotiations from the course we run, and having made such offers from my own budget in the past as a hiring manager (and having a CS degree myself with a few jobs in my career), I will give you a few possible reasons (in no particular order): But I believe, that more important question for you at this time is: what next?: If you must take this offer, then take it, get some real world experience, make some real contributions and ask for a raise. If they don’t give you a raise soon enough, then move on to a better company, better area, better role. Doing some strong interview preparation will increase your chances of putting a strong tech brand on your resume, after which you won’t ever have to ask this question again. Good luck!

Question: What is the best career advice for a software developer to earn a higher salary?

So, welcome to my world and hear me out! (No, not about smoking, but the greenback :-)). We have helped many candidates from Coding Interview Bootcamp negotiate compensation. First, let me state my assumptions: Now let me tell you what I consider “high” compensation. Obviously, anything more than what you make now is better, but it’s useful to have asymptotic numbers in mind, because depending on the time and era, those are different. As of this writing (late 2016), based on my experience, I’d consider the following yearly compensation as “high”, for a Software Engineer role. From the bootcamp, we have seen even higher comp in some of these categories, but you’ll have to agree, that for individual contributor roles, even these numbers are already high (if not very high). And obviously, by definition, not everyone gets to or even wants to optimize careers for high pay. Now let’s break it down i.e. understand different parts of a software engineer’s compensation: Now let’s understand different things that affect your compensation, and how to maximize them: Other things that affect your overall earnings: Lastly, while this was not a part of the question, I’d like to point out that this question is very dependent on what phase of life you are in. In my personal opinion (and mine only), your ideal career trajectory as a programmer, as maximized for money and fulfillment, is the following: Phase -1: In college, and right out of college (roughly years 17 through 25): work for a strong tech brand (could be Google or Facebook, but better if it’s a high growth smaller company). Nothing sets your life up for higher compensation, than working for a strong tech brand early in your career. Nothing. Phase-2: Years 22 to ~35: Work for a series of startups, big and small, as founder or early engineer. You’ll very likely do well with one or two of them. Phase-3: Years ~35+: If you want to remain an individual contributor, then prefer a big company, where you can spend the next 15+ years, while your social life takes equal priority. Question: Which are the 10 algorithms every computer science student must implement at least once in life?

Algorithms so pervasive in things we pickup every day, yet a normal person doesn’t know they exist, and we didn’t even do them in our CS courses! Why not implement them, just for fun? Just for gratitude? I’m going to list a few of those below. Not “top 10”, or “best 10”, but “tantalizing 10”, or just “reasonable 10”. I’m also going to avoid the obvious ones e.g. Binary searches and hash tables. And I’ll avoid some super esoteric ones, like say Krylov. Some of these are so within reach, that they even form actual coding interview questions! Hope you find them as much fun as I did. Question: Which tech company interviews are still hard to crack in Silicon Valley as on Sep 2016?
Answer: (Thanks for A2A Chockalingam Eswaramurthy) tl;dr: Best you can do, is segment companies by tiers of difficulty in interviewing. It’s practically not possible and futile even, to compare meaningfully within a given tier. Detail: Context: So as of Sept 2016, for past 2 years, I run an interview preparation bootcamp (Coding Interview Bootcamp) in the heart of Silicon Valley. We have had 300+ engineers take the program and may of them have gotten fantastic jobs all across the country. By way of that experience, we have a pretty good pulse on what’s technically challenging in interviews and what’s not. At least in the valley. First, let’s talk about the question and its assumptions: This is an interesting question, but seems to be framed in haste and with some unwarranted definitives. As a result, it contains several assumptions, which may not hold water: Assumption-1: Interview difficulty is comparable and measurable across companies “Interview difficulty” has no universal measure of it, nor a universal grade, like a standardized test does. And there won’t be any either, ever, because interviews are not standardized tests. There are more like a date, than they are like a test. It doesn’t make sense to have a universal measure of “hotness” of a person when it comes to relationships. That’s not how dating (interviews) work. Assumption-2: It is possible to generalize interview difficulty at a particular company. No, it’s not. Every company has different interview processes. Some are centralized, some are not. Some are language specific, some are not. Some are domain specific, some are not. Some are influenced strongly by a hiring manager, some are not. Some are influenced by the VP of the org, some are influenced by the CTO, some by recruiting department, some by a 3rd party and some are just done rudderless. We’ve seen Uber/Google/Facebook/LinkedIn/Amazon/Apple interviews ALL over the place. Some were hard, some were easy. Some were in the middle. Not to mention interview difficulty varies by seniority. Assumption-3: It is possible to know interview processes of all possible companies It’s not. Interview process is not standardized at most companies. It is moving target. Continually changes. Also, there is simply no enumeration of all possible tech companies. Assumption-4: Difficulty measure is same for all candidates It’s not. What I may find hard, you may not. I’ve also had instances where candidates weren’t able to crack seemingly easy companies, but cracked into Google. Assumption-5: Chasing companies with hardest interview processes is a good thing to do No it’s not. You haven’t claimed that directly, but it’s implied. I just want to clarify, that companies with hardest interviews don’t necessarily have best of offers, or best working environment. There is no general correlation like that. Now, let’s try and answer a more appropriate question: The best you can do, is to enumerate companies that have a “generally difficult interview process”. You already know that list: Google, Facebook, Palantir, Dropbox, Palantir, Uber, AirBnB, Quora, Snapchat etc. Occasionally we hear about MemSQL also. Also realize that there have been many engineers who have left Google (Uber, FB, etc), who are now a part of other companies and they have taken their interview chops with them. So I’m sure there are many many companies in the valley, who have a similarly challenging interview process. Having said that, we’ve had challenging interviews at companies like Intuit and Cisco also, who you wouldn’t otherwise consider to be difficult ones. But those are not “generally difficult” in comparison. i.e. the best you can do, is define tiers of difficulty like that: Tier-1 difficulty: the list above of G, F etc. (not many companies in this list) Tier-2 difficulty: Amazon, Apple, Microsoft etc. (probably a long list) Tier-3 difficulty: Everyone else (certainly a very long list) Also note, that tiering with interview difficulty has no solid correlation to business success of the company. We’ve seen amazing successes and failures coming out of all tiers. Now, let’s look at some specific examples from the question and outside: Has Google’s interview level gone down? Maybe, but there are no sure signs of it. Google is struggling to maintain its destination as a top employer for engineers compared to the newcomers (Uber, AirBnB, Snapchat and even Facebook), but it still remains the mecca of large scale engineering. Google engineers still get all benefit of doubt pretty much all across the world. Has Quora’s interview level gone down? Compared to Google, Quora is very tiny and they do far fewer interviews. If it’s difficult to tell about G’s level, it’s probably impossible to tell how Quora’s level has changed. From what I can tell, it shouldn’t have changed at all. There are some roles where they may be lenient, but for core software engineering roles, they can’t afford to let loose at this early stage. Has Apple’s interview level gone down? Fortune 3 company. And it doesn’t show up in top-tier? Well, it may. Depends on which team you’re interviewing for. We’ve seen Apple interviews to be all over the place. At some places, they do domain specific interviews and some places they do language specific interviews. And of course, in some teams they do Algorithms based interviews. Not possible to put a general feeling on it. Has Uber’s interview level gone down? Uber has grown very very fast (faster than what G was at this size) and they have struggled to maintain a good control over their interview process, and more importantly they have struggled to maintain good control over their culture too. As a result, the interview experiences are quite varied. I wouldn’t say it has gone down though, when nobody knows what was ‘up’. Hope this helps!

Question: What are the best tips for negotiating a compensation package at Google? What should someone know about the way these aspects of compensation will be paid out? What are typical baselines for a program manager and how negotiable are these terms?
Answer: We often negotiate Google offers for candidates from our programs. Here is what we have learnt: 1. Google DOES negotiate. It absolutely does. I respect Bob See’s perspective, but from what we have seen, lately Google has started to budge. They are losing a lot of engineers to Uber and Snapchat, which has made them realize that they need to up their game. 2. Google does not negotiate, if offers are from random-ass companies. In order to move the needle at Google, you need to have competing offers. Good, competing offers from public companies, or pre-IPO companies. Think Uber, Facebook. 3. It depends a LOT on your recruiter. Some recruiters are very seasoned, and they play this psychological war very well. It’s very difficult to negotiate if you are caught with one of those. But other recruiters are more vulnerable. 4. They DO sign on bonuses. Hefty ones sometimes. Sign-on bonuses only happen when you have had a great interview, you get an exceptional fit with a team, and thus they REALLY want to attract you. It doesn’t happen otherwise. 5. Google CAN play evil. Yes, despite their motto. It’s rare, but it does happen. We once had an offer made at Level 3 for a candidate who was on the cusp of 3 and 4. The candidate declined, because they had other better offers (Uber, Dropbox) at higher levels. Despite having full knowledge of other competing offers, Google waited until last minute, and only then offered Level 4, with the condition that the candidate sign the new offer as is, or they will be barred forever from interviewing with Google. You guessed it - it was a seasoned recruiter. In summary, if you have no competing offers from proper companies, and you really want Google, then you are pretty much at the mercy of your recruiter. They might move a bit if you persist and insist, but not much. In order to get something more meaningful out of them you need a strong competing offer. And a degree in psychology if your recruiter is seasoned.
