Question: What lame things do programmers often argue about?
Answer: Programmers (claimer: I’m one) tend to argue about a lot of lame things (tabs vs spaces, placement of braces, naming of variables, number of return statements, parameter passing etc). But know that bickering on lame things is not a privilege of programmers. There are parallels in every profession. So much so, that unlike other kinds of bickering, this even is a named law for it! It’s very appropriately called the Law of Triviality. Quoting Wikipedia: Parkinson's law of triviality is C. Northcote Parkinson's 1957 argument that members of an organisation give disproportionate weight to trivial issues. He observed that a committee whose job was to approve the plans for a nuclear power plant spent the majority of its time on discussions about relatively minor but easy-to-grasp issues, such as what materials to use for the staff bike-shed, while neglecting the proposed design of the plant itself, which is far more important but also a far more difficult and complex task. The law has been applied to software development and other activities. The term bike-shedding or the bike-shed effect was coined as a metaphor to illuminate the law of triviality; it was popularised in the Berkeley Software Distribution community by the Danish computer developer Poul-Henning Kamp in the mid-1990s and has spread from there to the whole software industry. Poul-Hemming Kamp even has an almost entertaining and emotional webpage for it: bikeshed.com. If you refresh that page, you will get a different background color each time. I like blue. It’s the best. All other colors are the worst. Blue makes everything better. How can you not see that? You’re colorblind. Now refresh that page! Again. Wait for blue.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What can I do to get better at algorithms? I'm a pretty good programmer, I use LeetCode, and I've tried implementing data structures in languages. What more can I do?
Answer: Context: I run an intense bootcamp to prepare for technical interviews. A large part of what we do, is problem-solving with DS and Algos. Let me share a few lessons we’ve learnt. If you’re spending 2–3 hours on Leetcode for a number of days, you’re bound to get better. There are no two ways about it. Practice is the only way anyone gets better at this (or anything else for that matter). So if I had to wager, I’d say you are probably decent at DS/A already and that’s not your problem; your problem is likely in reproducing that skill in an interview. Here are a few guesses, along with what you can do about each: Deep-down, you are confused about whether you want to remain a software engineer That’s a bold and slightly rude statement for me to make - I apologize. But from what you say above, one clear possibility I discern, is that you don’t see yourself as a software-engineer, whose primary satisfaction comes from doing an air-tight technical design and writing solid code. Please don’t get me wrong - every engineer has to care about design and product very much, but that is not their primary role. Their pride usually comes from making the best technical decisions, and not from making the best UX or Business decisions. Here are the phrases that tell me that you may be confused: “work … to get access to users” “… I do market research” “understand the people who will be using my apps” “I feel like my value comes from my not just being an engineer, but someone who thinks about design and the product as a whole” These are all the things that a founder has to do, so if you meant those in that context, then I do apologize. But otherwise, to me, this is a telltale sign. What can you do: Unless you’re certain about this and I’m wrong, you have to make a decision. If your mind continues to gravitate to areas other than how to make the best technical decisions, it may be time to make hard choices. You may make a good product manager or founder, while using your technical skills to differentiate yourself from the pack. You fail to see the point of DS/A in interviews You have probably never stopped and asked/researched why the technical interview process is dominated by DS/A and why more and more companies are jumping on that bandwagon. There are several reasons for it, but the main one, is that for companies, it’s the most convenient way to interview at scale and compare candidates. What can you do: I’ll elaborate that and other reasons in another post, but it would be awesome if next time you see a DS/A question, you have faith that it’s probably the least evil method to interview, if not the best. And that your interviewer, however well meaning they were, have not had much of a choice in grand scheme of things. Unless you do that, you’ll carry an anxiety that’ll annoy you nearly every time in an interview. You are not repeating the problems you’ve done It’s not sufficient to do a problem once and feel happy about it. While it’s important to internalize and fully understand a problem, it’s equally important to work your recall circuitry. What can you do: Repeat the problems you’ve done, or find and do very similar ones. Not necessary to write code, but you have to load the same problems in your head every few days. If you do competitive programming on sites like TopCoder or CodeForces or similar, you’ll find a cluster of similar problems more easily. Repeating will increase your confidence as well as understanding. You haven’t done enough problems What can you do: Try hitting about 150 problems, or about half of Leetcode. That will start to move the needle. If you’re at 50 or so, that’s warmup. At about 100, it starts to get better. You are not doing practice interviews Unlike a college exam, Interviews are open-ended. The only way to get better at open-ended stuff, is with continual feedback from right people. Without feedback, there is no grade or score you will get in technical interviews, which will tell you whether you’re getting better, or whether you’re driving down a cliff. What can you do: When in practice mode, every few days, do some mock interviews, or do real interviews at practice companies. Keep calibrating yourself continually, outside of real interviews. That will also increase your confidence. Hope this helps!

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: I constantly get stuck on technical programming interview questions unable to progress. Is there a way that I can practice and actually get better?
Answer: [Obligatory context and disclaimer: I run an intense, one-of-a-kind and successful bootcamp focused on preparing for Tech interviews: http://interviewkickstart.com . Nearly 200 engineers have gone through the program since inception. We keenly observe how candidates practice and progress] Practice is the only way you'll get better. There is no other way anyone gets better at anything, much less interviewing. There are plenty of resources available for practice. viz. Books, Websites, Meetups, our course etc. A few things are important to know: 1. You have to stick to your practice. Diligently. It's surprisingly difficult to stick to simple habits, but that's often the difference between success and failure. e.g. 2-4 hours a day to solve one or two problems is a great habit: necessary and often sufficient. But it's imperative that you actually do so several days a week for a number of weeks, rain or shine, in order to get cumulative benefits. 2. Recall is critical and you need continual feedback via mock interviews Interviews are not standardized tests. You can't prepare for them in a vacuum for several months and then suddenly hope to get better at the end of it all. That could work for SAT prep, but not for non-standardized tests like technical interviews, where grading is not standardized. After every few problems/days of practice, you have to do mock interviews. Mock interviews are best done with engineers at top companies, but they can also be done with your friends and fellow seekers. Mocks will help your recall circuitry, and give you feedback about where you stand. That will in turn, either increase your confidence, or let you tweak your practice early, if required. 3. You need to write code Just skimming problems and loading the solutions in your head is unlikely to be enough. Writing code is important in order to make the solutions real. When you write code, you will also discover and learn a lot of nuances of the programming language you're using, which will come handy in actual interviews and elsewhere. 4. You need to repeat the problems Repetition deepens your understanding of problems and their solutions. Often patterns emerge only after repeating a number of problems. Obviously, repetition also improves recall and gives confidence. 5. Don't look for a magical moment of end viz. "I'm ready" Thumb rule is to reach about 150 medium to challenging problems as your first milestone. I've seen people cross 300 also. By that time, assuming you've written code for those many problems and repeated them, you should feel pretty confident. But overall, let mock interviews guide your prep. 6. Practice with a long term goal Practice with a long term goal of being a better engineer. Interview problems will do that for you viz. actually make you a better coder and system-design-er. That will in turn, make your short-term goal of getting a job more realistic, and less agonizing. Good luck!

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What are the best-kept secrets about startups?
Answer: Your success is more dependent on your skills in messaging, than it's on access to money or strategy. Your initial customers will come because they believe in you and your vision. That comes when you can effectively communicate what you offer. Your initial hires are also going to come because they believe in your and your vision. They are going to be inspired by what you say and how you say it. Your investors are going to be the same. Your acquisition is dependent on how you've presented yourself in the industry, which in turn depends on what you say and how you say it. Once you start on an idea you're passionate about, you'll notice that you'll need to experiment with how to explain it properly. It can take several tries, and often months, to get to a narrative that generally works. If you can get to a narrative that works reliably with just a certain kind of audience (one distribution channel), then that is the first turning point of your business. It's not about marketing blasts on facebook; it's about nailing one distribution channel with precise messaging. Having the runway and perseverance to survive until you cycle through different distribution channels, and nail that narrative with one, with a high-enough conversion rate (even 10% is great), is the difference between really getting off the ground, and not. In fact, despite iterating several times, if you are finding it difficult to nail your messaging for a given audience, that may be your earliest indication that product-market fit is going to be very difficult. Messaging is that powerful secret, in plain sight.

Question: To those of you who interviewed for a software engineering role at Google, Facebook, Amazon and got in without preparing for the interview, will you share your experience?
Answer: Context and disclaimer: I run an intense and successful bootcamp focused on preparing for Tech interviews. A 100+ people from all over the world have prepped with us since we started a year and a half ago: http://interviewkickstart.com We've since learnt a lot about what makes successful engineers. While nearly everyone who goes thru us (and is actively looking) gets placed somewhere nice, the people who crack some of the hardest interviews generally fall into ONE or MORE of the following categories: 1. They are just bright from the get go. A high IQ. These are your friends who you have always wondered how easily they "get" things. They come up with keen observations the fastest. They can get by with normal amount of practice viz. brush-up. Not saying they are the happiest people on the planet, but they often don't need the kind of prep you and I do. 2. They are extremely prepped. Extremely. A crude measure of prep, is how many data-structures/algorithmic problems you've practiced. Some of these people have crossed 300+ problems. Written code for each. And repeated it. It takes several months to a year to do this with diligence and focus. 3. They have been coding for a long time. Almost precocious-ly. They have written so much code, that a lot of constructs are now muscle memory. All they need to do in an interview, is to intuit the solution. After that, they impress the heck with their coding fluency. 4. They are competitive programmers for some time. They don't have to be toppers or winning competitions. e.g. Yellow on Topcoder is sufficient. 5. They went to a particularly strong and competitive CS program Some programs in the country prepare you for such interviews. Rare, and difficult to get into, but they do. 6. They got a soft interview-panel. Interviews are heavily dependent on who interviews you. At large companies, there is a wide variance in grading standard, experience in interviewing and in beliefs, and hence there is a wide variation in intake bar, despite centralized hiring committees. You need a bit of luck anyway, but sometimes you get an entire panel that you happen to gel with. A little bit of preparation and getting such a panel puts you over the magic line. Lesson? Prepare. You'll be glad you did. Not because it just might get you a ticket to some of the best gravy trains on the planet, but because the right kind of interview preparation actually makes you a better engineer in your daily work.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: I see 25-year-old developers being offered crazy salaries, like $150 - 200k, in such companies as Google, Facebook, Apple, etc. How can I become highly skilled to qualify for such offers, if I have no formal education but am a web developer?
Answer: Congratulations on taking the leap to proactively ask this question in the first place. I'm so glad you said: How can I grow as a programmer, instead of some lazy, shortcut-y thing. Like Coach Paul Bryant says: Everyone wants to win, but very few want to prepare to win. The central advice I will give you, is to approach this systematically, and make a plan. Given your particular situation (not a traditional CS background, limited experience, not in US), it is unlikely for you to easily get such interviews and crack them. You'll likely need a longer runway, and more patience than your counterparts with traditional CS background and/or experience. Start asking and answering some of these questions top-down, with the end goal of creating a plan: 1. Is your goal really to make more money by being a better engineer, or do you just want to make a lot of money? To know what you really want, is a surprisingly hard question to answer. Smart people can often see themselves succeeding at most things, which leads to analysis-paralysis and subsequent inaction. I'd urge you to think through this clearly. If you just want to make 250K a year, then there are relatively easier ways (mostly by starting a small business). 2. What kind of companies offer these salaries and where are they? What is the typical salary/equity breakdown? In free economies, Salaries are a function of supply and demand, and not value or skill. In the US, the demand for software-engineers is very high, compared to its supply, and hence the salaries are high (while Primary school teachers are paid pittance). Not sure how it is in your country, and if you're planning to move. Many companies offer these packages, but the breakdown of Salary and Equity depends on what stage the company is in. Big companies (think G, F etc) currently offer north of 200K+ a year to entry-level engineers, but the breakdown is 60+/40- (salary/equity). The balance is about 50/50 in pre-IPO companies (think Uber, AirBnB etc). In smaller startups, it's often 30/70. You need to answer this question based on your geographic location and feasibility/willingness to move. 3. What kind of experience and education do engineers at these companies have? What are the exceptions? One thing you'll notice here, is that there are many more engineers working in semi-engineering roles, compared to core engineering roles. Semi-engineering roles are excellent for starters. They often come with similar salaries and amazing visibility into core engineering. They can also be slightly easier to get into e.g. Solutions engineering, Support engineering etc. Core engineering roles often go to engineers with very specific experience and/or traditional CS background. While that is changing, and I've seen excellent self-taught engineers from coding bootcamps go into these roles, but it's often in their 2nd or 3rd job. Another area where self-taught engineers go a lot, is Technical Operations. With massive shift happening to Cloud, those roles are also evolving into traditional engineering roles, but there are still many entry-level openings there. There is a lot more to say here, but your research needs to be tailored to your geographical location and availability. 4. How do you get interviews at such companies? Getting interviews is as much of a problem, as clearing them. I often see candidates under-estimating this. Don't apply online. Your background doesn't stand a clear chance, vis-a-vis other applications. Go through head-hunters and referrals. Rattle your networks, and build connections. You'll need a number of interviews before you get a couple of good offers. 5. What does the interview process look like? Look up sites like Glassdoor (or equivalent in your country), to understand what's at stake. Reach out to recruiters and engineers working at these companies for informational chats. Ask about their interview process. You'll likely find that they are surprisingly open. 6. What does it take to crack those interviews? Depending on the position and company you're applying for, it may take anywhere from weeks to months, in order to prepare. Often, the processes at these places are fraught with Data Structures and Algorithms questions. Those can take a lot of time to get good at. Fortunately there are a lot of resources available for it, but they all take time (books, websites, courses, bootcamp). If you notice that interviews are mostly (or also) about a certain programming language, then your prep will need to focus in that direction. And of course, all this assumes that you have good communication skills, which can be very important in getting interviews as well as clearing them. Like any other skill, that can also be improved very much, but you'll need to factor that time in your plan. In summary, you'll probably notice that it's less about knowing a specific language. It's about knowing what's realistic, what companies and roles to aim for, and then do targeted preparation for those. You want to end with a list of about 50 companies that you can reach out to, get initial technical screening interviews at 20 of them (those that offer these salaries, are in your physical reach, where you clearly know the roles you're targeting, and the interview prep is within your runway), get on-site interviews at about 8-10, which will result in 2 or more offers. Once you get a couple of offers, you negotiate with them, pick the best, and enjoy the ride :-) Good luck! [I make these observations by way of running a focused, rigorous and successful bootcamp on technical interview preparation: Coding Interview Bootcamp. Taught by practicing engineers at top-tier companies, we firmly believe that most engineers are good, and only interviews stand in their way]

Question: Is it possible to read and solve problems from CLRS in 1 month for person with no CS degree, with avg. knowledge in math & good problem-solving skills

Question: What is the most unfair advantage a person can have?
Answer: "most unfair advantage" is very context-sensitive: So on and so forth. If this is a high-level question, about creating the most unfair advantage, then I believe it's: Obsession. (Obviously, we're talking about positive obsession, and not the clinical condition). A lot has been written about Success and Expertise. [An excellent summary can be found here]. One thing that most of these studies agree on, is that successful people were neither necessarily talented, nor necessarily born to wealthy parents, but they all necessarily obsessed with improving themselves to achieve their goals. Not just motivated, but obsessed. If the question however is about the most unfair advantage that is bestowed (and not in your hands), then by far it is: being born to loving parents in the right place at the right time. That gives a head-start and a level of confidence in life which nothing else does.

Question: What skills do software engineers have who make over $400,000 per year?
Answer: I know several engineers who make 400K+ a year. They all fall into one of the following buckets: 1. They got rich by startup equity They were either very early (first engineer) or founders of successful startups that got acquired or went public. 2. They got counter-offers from their employers Google engineers getting Facebook offers or vice-versa (and then forcing their company to give them a better counter offer) was relatively common a few years ago, and still happening. 3. They have been at large, successful companies for a long time, and got rich by refresher grants: Refresher grants (the ones you get every year after joining a company) are sizable at companies like Google and Apple. So after say 6 years or so, you can start cashing out many of your RSUs and your pay is comfortably over 400K. 4. They are into mid to upper level management at successful companies They are not coding at work, but they are still engineers at heart and by education. So, you see: Above all though, they are all good engineers. They care about their craft. They pour themselves into their work with an obsession and with a vengeance. It is with those skills, that they have gotten lucky.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why are most developers of Silicon Valley tech companies in their 20s and 30s? Where are the older developers?
Answer: I'm in my late 30s, but hopefully I am "old enough" to answer this question :-) Older developers in Silicon Valley, are mostly: 1. Deep into the bowels of big companies: The kind of companies that were pinnacles of career at one point, but are not as jazzy anymore e.g. IBM or Cisco. These big companies have hired thousands of developers over the years, and provided them stable, long-lasting careers. 2. OR they have moved into management: By definition, there are fewer managers than there are developers. Some have also moved on to Product Management, or Entrepreneurship or have left Silicon Valley to cheaper areas. And some immigrants have returned to their home countries after a successful half of their career in the US. The elephant in the room however, is that there just are not that many "older" developers. That is simply because programming (and computing tech in general), was not in such high demand 20+ years ago (I pick that time because kids opting for programming at/before that time would be 40+ today, which is the demographic we're wondering about). It is now that every taxi and toothbrush company needs programmers. Two decades ago, only "software" companies needed programmers and there weren't very many of those. As a result, programming wasn't a thing "back then". One had to make a conscious choice to route their career into it. At the time, top kids from high-school usually went into Medicine or other kinds of engineering viz. Chemical or Mechanical, which were perceived to be in higher and longer-term demand. When I decided to opt for CS as my major in 1996 (20 years ago!), I remember getting so much advice against it. My choice of CS was routinely pitied and it was common to hear things around the theme of: "Did you study that hard in high-school to get into computers? Really?". I had to remain consciously stubborn to stick with my choice, against the will of my (well-meaning) parents and friends. I can imagine the choice being much harder to make for developers more senior than I am. [Edit: Restructured the flow of thoughts]

Question: How important is it to get a Computer Science degree at a larger, well-known college?
Answer: Having worked with, interviewed and coached countless software engineers so far, here is what I now firmly believe in: Presence of a strong brand name on your resume early in your career, has a long-lasting influence and pays dividends forever. I can't emphasize this enough. i.e. Pick the school that has a stronger brand name in Computer Science. Check the rankings, and/or ask some technical recruiters to find out. Yes, it doesn't always mean that CS grads from brand name schools are better trained; at the end of the day, it's very much on the individual (you). But engineers with stronger resumes will have more conversations opened to them, than engineers otherwise. Shelling out $15K may feel a little too high at the moment, but it's negligible compared to the salary elevation and other non-tangible benefits you'll get over a 40 year career. If you are sure to be sticking to CS, then go for a stronger school despite the tuition. Same goes for the company you work for after college. Starting your career with a better company elevates your career trajectory in a way that nothing else does. [Edited after reading the exact numbers]

Question: Am I "owed" interview feedback? I interviewed at Facebook and thought it went well, but they sent me a form rejection letter and didn't respond to my polite request for feedback. I don't want to keep making the same mistakes. Is that unreasonable?
Answer: It was 2007, and I was at eBay. I was conducting a technical phone-screen. The candidate wasn't doing particularly well with the questions. After about 45 minutes, I wrapped it with these words: "Hey, it was great talking to you!", put my notes into the system, and then went on with my daily stuff. What followed, was somewhat hilarious and bizarre. After the candidate got his rejection, he was furious. He called HR and asked why he was rejected, even though "the interviewer said it was great talking to me!". He couldn't make sense of the fact that it was simply a courtesy and even though it was indeed great talking to him, that didn't mean he did well in the interview. The recruiter had to go take permission from the lawyer before sending him my (redacted) feedback. But that didn't pacify him either. He went over the recruiter's head, to his manager and everyone he could find. He persisted for several weeks with one silly reason or another, demanding "the answer". Eventually, the position got filled with an internal transfer, after which he stopped. Isolated case, you say? Of course. But look at how much time and effort we had to sink into it. That's the tragedy with giving feedback (and many other things in life). 1% of isolated irrational cases take 99% of time and 101% of mindshare. Sorry, however genuine your reason is, and however well meaning the interviewers are, a fair system of giving feedback unfortunately just doesn't scale (and we must create something that works at scale). Don't expect it; you're not owed any. PS: Realize that even colleges don't give us feedback when they reject us. That, despite taking an application fee. And despite us having spent years trying to get into one. PPS: Nobody owes you feedback even when you clear the interview. Most people don't care about feedback on success, but the point is, that it's very hard to give feedback even when it's positive. The right way to look at an interview, is like a date, and not like a standardized test. The more you think about interviews like the latter, the more you will agonize about feedback and scoring and such. It doesn't work that way. [Major edits: Added PS and things after that]

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What do you disagree with in Cracking the Coding Interview?
Answer: Don't shoot the messenger (the books). Nothing to disagree with the book. That book (and books like that, online websites, our bootcamp etc) are simply filling a need. They are responding to what technical interviewing is these days. [And what most CS colleges have failed to deliver viz. really preparing their grads for the real world; but that's a different topic for a different day]. We could disagree with the process of technical interviewing, but don't shoot the messenger (the books et al). 1. An unfortunate side-effect of that book and other prep material, is that they now have provided a lot more options to interviewERS to ask questions from. As a result, as someone who is preparing for interviews, and targeting these coveted companies, you feel like doing more and more problems. And as a result, the typical process of preparing for these kinds of technical interviews, has become longer and harder. [Whether interviewers should take the questions from that book directly or not, is also a different question for a different time; suffice to realize though, that interviewers are also human and coming up with new questions is hard]. 2. Another consequence of such books and sites, is that it has become easier for companies to perpetuate the current technical interview process. It has made the companies less thoughtful about their own interviews. It shouldn't be that way; nobody is forcing the companies to be less thoughtful, but they see an easy out and a printed legitimacy. i.e. It becomes very easy to say "that book has an excellent problem; let's ask something that!" vs. "What kind of person do we exactly need and what kind of questions will help us get to that". Current process of interviewing exists for a reason and there are pros and cons to it. Books and sites were not meant to subtly legitimize them in all situations. But again, interviewers are humans. And that's what I see.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: How much do interns contribute to the growth of a tech company?
Answer: I've hired and worked with many software engineering interns in my career. When does it work out? If an intern is hired with a specific project in mind, and the hiring bar is kept reasonably high, it usually works out very well. Their contribution is about the same as a good full-time employee's. Strong candidates filtering in through a high bar, are often very good programmers from strong CS backgrounds. With decent mentoring, you can trust them to do and produce important work quickly. That's an excellent way to catch good engineers early, before they hit the regular job market and get usurped by your competition. Also, depending on the time and location, hiring interns can also give a business tax-credits from local governments. When does it not work? If a company is hiring the "proverbial" interns, with a low bar, without a specific goal or deadline, just to get some orphaned grunt work done, it's very difficult to justify their contribution, if at all. If the company is hiring interns in lieu of full-time employees with the primary goal of saving money in the short term, even then it doesn't usually work in the long term, leading to negative value creation.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why does everyone want to work at Google and not Microsoft even if they have similar perks and benefits?
Answer: If people joined companies primarily for its perks & benefits, we'd see an arms race in perks & benefits and this world would have been a very different place :-) Assuming you're talking about software engineers, if I were to make the choice today, here is how I'd think: There are exceptions though. If I'm getting to join a better team at Microsoft, then I'd prefer to join Microsoft. Again, nothing to do with perks and benefits. But barring those exceptions, all things equal, usually people prefer to join a more modern company with a stronger, recognizable brand, that helps them further their careers. Between the two, Google is that company. Case in point: at Coding Interview Bootcamp, I get excellent engineers from Microsoft who want to prepare for interviews for companies like Google and others. But I don't get people from Google :-) At least not yet. Having said all this, let us also keep things in perspective: More often than not, most people do not have a choice in what company to join. They are just looking for a good job, and they accept the first decent one they land. Process of searching for a job is agonizing at best. If you are lucky enough to have offers from both Google and Microsoft, the first thing you should do, is to feel lucky. You're probably among the top 1%le of job seekers, and your hard work has paid off. Now go make your decision.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Can every CS professor pass Google's interview?
Answer: No. Software Engineering is a related, but different discipline from Computer Science. And technical interviewing is often an entirely different thing. John L. Miller has said everything I wanted to say. I'll just add one more validation to it: At our bootcamp (Coding Interview Bootcamp), we expressly do not hire professors to teach, for this exact reason. We hire awesome practicing engineers to teach technical problem solving skills. The perspective brought in by someone who spent 5+ years in thriving large-scale systems, is entirely different from that of an academic professor. And for interviews, it's far more relevant. It's also worth noting, that research isn't a privilege of universities these days. Google (and many large companies) funds and conducts joint research with a number of universities around the world. So the lines are blurring. For CS professors, that's another way to work with Google if they want to.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: How can I become a data scientist?
Answer: Whenever you're changing careers (e.g., whatever to Data Science) or pursuing something generally difficult to learn (e.g., competing for technical interviews at best companies), I highly recommend starting with a structured (interactive, time-bound, accountable) course. The question is never whether you can learn something new on your own. The question is always whether you can do it fast enough or faster than your competition. It’s relatively easy to find good material on anything new you want to learn in today’s world, whether it's cooking or data-science. You can see pointers to those in many excellent answers here. But that's not enough for most. Most people need a competitive advantage, especially in their careers. Your competitive advantage in today's world is less in finding the most comprehensive available material. It is how fast you can get through any material and how effectively you can understand the material. That's where a structured course helps. Learning with a teacher who has done this stuff many times before, in the company of talented peers, shortens your learning curve by a magnitude. That is actually when a challenging curriculum comes to life. You make fewer rookie-mistakes and are ready faster for a better role. Try a data-science Bootcamp or a masters' degree. Online or offline. There are some good ones out there, and you'll very likely find one in your budget. Simultaneously, try participating in competitions, on say, Kaggle. Or get some freelancing projects under your belt. You'll be on your way much faster than someone who doesn't follow a structured approach. Question: Why are so many people in software engineering obsessed about salary?
Answer: Herbert Lee nailed it. Let's also think a bit further: What's the root cause of parents sending kids to do Software Engineering, or Engineers getting funded for asinine ideas? or companies pampering engineers so much? Demand. Very high demand. And not enough supply. That sheer imbalance is driving up the "price" of a software engineer. And once my neighbor makes X doing the same work, why would I make less than X? We're in another Industrial Revolution, only this time we call it Digital Revolution. The way Manufacturing skill was in high demand during the 1700s and 1800s, Software Engineering is in high demand today. Every single thing we do, is rapidly getting digitized and internet-enabled. Case in point: 6 years ago, if I'd told you that a Taxi company will hire software engineers, you'd have laughed me off. Turns out, today, the days of starting a taxi company without having software engineers, are gone. Long gone, actually. At some point, Software Engineering will also get commoditized, just the way Manufacturing is commoditized today. We're already starting to see some of that, e.g. static webpages can be built on Upwork for <$5/hr. But whether mass commoditization will happen in 10 years or 100, is hard to reason. My guess, is that it'll probably be something like 2 generations (say ~50 years). Our grandkids, if they are software engineers, will not obsess about salary, because nobody will pay them that much. But then, we'll all find a way to send them to something else that'll be in high demand at the time. And then I'll be back to Quora to answer a freshly minted question about why people with that X skill are obsessed with ... you know :-) --- PS: I run Coding Interview Bootcamp for a living, and help candidates negotiate salaries. I hence know this situation better than I ever want to know. It's mind-boggling to see companies open up their wallets when you have multiple offers and you have aced the interviews. It's all about Demand and Supply. [Image source: https://circusventures.files.wordpress.com/2014/11/supply-and-demand.jpg ]

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Why didn't I get selected for Google? What should I do to improve my chances in future?
Answer: At Box, our interview process was very similar to Google's. (Probably a bit more thoughtful, because we were not hiring at that speed or magnitude) When I was a Director of Engineering there, I did a little personal experiment. At the end of every onsite interview for my team, I'd go meet the candidate and ask her/him how they thought the interview went (among other things). I'd find that the candidates had the wrong impression. nearly. every. single. time. They were clearly making judgments based on how the interviewer made them feel, and not on the objective merit of their answer. It's actually very difficult for any candidate to get an objective judgement on the merit of their answer in that short time, which is why s/he subconsciously relies on the interviewer to provide that signal. But interviewers are trained to not give you all feedback. They are trained to make you feel better, regardless of your answer. Especially the seasoned ones at good companies. In other words, your feeling that your interviews went well may not be complete/real. Your scores are decent, so you must have tried well, but not acceptable in their minds. But they didn't make you feel that way. Google has a brand enigma, so it's natural for candidates to aspire for it (and feel stung when they don't get in). But realize that there are many companies with equally strong technical teams, who'd love to have you. Whenever you're interviewing, always interview with a basket of companies in mind. After all, interviews are not standardized tests; they are more like a date. Except for your own preparation, who gets hired is not in your control. Remember to never pin your confidence on one single company. At Coding Interview Bootcamp, that's the underlying philosophy we have adopted.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Career-wise, which option is better, given limited time and the need to choose: open source contributions, or competitive programming?
Answer: Participants in Coding Interview Bootcamp often ask this question. I see the two paths as having somewhat complementary benefits: OSS contributions: If you pick the right project, you'll learn to write better, cleaner code (not necessarily faster), that's broadly acceptable. You'll learn to organize and document your code better, which is a critical skill. You'll gain meaningful experience on your resume, which will lead to more interviews at good companies, whatever your experience or education level is. After you get hired, it'll be easier to positively and strongly differentiate yourselves from other software engineers in your company. Competitive programming: You'll learn to code faster, not necessarily better. You'll get a much better understanding of Data Structures and Algorithms. If you win competitions, you will be able to put it on your resume and get more interviews. You'll also likely fly through Data Structures and Algorithms-type interviews, whatever your experience or education level is. After you get hired though, you'll probably need to adapt yourself, because you'll realize that speed isn't the most important part of coding in an organization. It's design, organization and readability. Whatever choice you make, I'd urge you to make it with the right intent: Intent of OSS contribution: Is to pay it forward. i.e. genuinely contribute to OSS, to which we all owe our existence. Intent of Competitive Programming: Is self-improvement via programming challenges. In either path, career-oriented benefits will come relatively soon, but it will take a while to make good on the final intent.

Question: Why do Microsoft software engineers tend to stay for a long time compared to other tech companies?
Answer: Steven Grimm and John L. Miller have nailed it. Here is one more (supplementing) reason (assuming you interviewed in Seattle WA and are comparing to what you've heard of Bay Area): The culture there is simply not like Bay Area. In the Bay, the socially acceptable maximum to stay at a company has been steadily reducing over the years. These days, it's about 4-6 years, based on my experience. i.e. if you stayed somewhere longer than 6-7 years, you should expect that someone will ask you about it. And, the next time you meet them, they'll likely be working for some other company, because the first one folded. This makes you think if you're doing the right thing staying longer at your employer. Prediction: It's going to change for Microsoft too. Seattle is changing, so is Microsoft and the concept of long careers is dwindling. Big companies are no longer safe havens for a long career.

Question: I make $110 K per year as a senior software developer. Should I leave for the sake of professional development? I am bored. I received offers from BlackBerry and IBM, but my current employer offered me a better package each time.
Answer: tl;dr: I like your introspection. I'd suggest you rethink your opinion of not working at the tech giants you name. And regardless of whether you want to join them, you should prepare for interviews, as if you were to interview there. Just preparing for interviews will re-energize you and challenge you to be a better engineer. Longer answer: I happen to hold a unique perspective to your exact situation largely due to my profession: Coding Interview Bootcamp. I talk to many people people in your boat every week viz. Smart people, who are not challenged at work. Congratulations on being that introspective. You will be surprised how rare the skill of introspection is. Especially when it comes to career progression, most people don't realize what you've realized, until it's too late. Given you're introspective and you clearly know what's missing at work, I'd urge you to go a little further and ask, where will you find such work? That will take you to more introspection about what you want out of your career. I can't tell you what you'll eventually want/like, but below, I'll give you a generalization based on my experience and experience of several other people: Given that you're a software engineer, you'll find exciting and challenging work at places that are solving technical problems that are not solved before. (If something has been solved for a few years, you'll invariably find it on blogs and on Stackoverflow, or wrapped in some API documentation) Typically, challenging technical advances are found in teams that deal with products on a world consumer scale (e.g. Google, Facebook, Netflix, LinkedIn, Snapchat etc). Or they are found at places that are doing deeply fundamental work, bordering research (e.g. Tesla). I'm sure there are other examples, but these are the two biggest categories. There are many consumer tech companies and companies that have scaled their products out there, but the scaling problems with products that have to reach every user on the planet, are just not solved yet. e.g. Before Big Table was written, you couldn't have Googled for it. (Again, not all teams at these places to challenging work. You need to seek out the ones that do) You'll generally find, that when you work in these teams, you're challenged more, and you're happier, even though you're working more. Yes, people do leave those companies too, but it's usually not because of non-challenging work. You'll also find that all these companies ask you Data Structures, Algorithms and System Design problems in their interviews. Now ask yourself: why is that? Engineers at these companies are not dumb. They know that they are not doing DS and Algorithms at work every day. Then why have they been asking these problems for years and years? Why is it that so many other companies have replicated that method? There are many reasons for it. A big one, is that it's probably the fastest method to find engineers who are deeply interested in their profession, engineers who are reasonably intelligent and engineers who work hard to tackle hard problems - all at the same time. This method filters out a lot of good people unnecessarily, but so will every method. It's not the only way, but it's one way. i.e. What I'm suggesting, is you re-think your opinion on working at these companies. Prepare hard for interviews while you're employed. Leave only when you get into one of these good ones. After you get in, find your groove, and attain a certain trust level to maintain a work-life balance. And even if you don't want to leave your existing workplace, I'd suggest you prepare for interviews, as if you were to interview at these companies. Just interview preparation will challenge you enough to be a better engineer. Overall, people like you, who are introspective and see themselves succeeding in multiple paths, IMHO, should overcome such dilemmas based on Regret Minimization Framework: Some follow this advice, take the leap and start preparing for interviews, while some decide to stay put. People in the former group have never regretted the decision. Interview preparation can happen in many ways. There are excellent books, meetups, websites and now our bootcamp. Whichever route you'll go - you'll be glad you did.

Question: I've been struggling with Cracking the Coding problems. How do I get better at these problems?
Answer: Cracking the Coding Interview (2011 book) is a very good book. It's sincerely written and the 6th edition also has hints. The best way to get better, is to not lose patience and stay with the problem. However long it takes. Write code for it yourself, copy-paste model code from Github and debug the hell out of it, etc. You're bound to get better. It may be slower at first, but if you don't lose patience, you will get better. While you're with a problem, feel free to Google the problem. Many problems have excellent explanations online. As you stay with a problem, you'll slowly realize the gaps in your understanding e.g. if you're not able to grasp tree traversals, then go learn that first. There are plenty of resources for those basics. If you need help, start with a colleague or a friend or a classmate (if you're a student) or a meetup (www.meetup.com). You could also look for a course, where you have access to excellent teachers and interviewers. e.g. We run one: Coding Interview Bootcamp , though we have our own material. It's an intermediate to advanced course, targeting core engineering roles at top-tier companies. Hope this helps.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: How important is one's school's prestige in the interview process for tech companies?
Answer: It's important in getting an interview; not so much after you get one. I've been to both kinds of schools when I was at Box. And at Coding Interview Bootcamp , we have trained highly experienced as well as fresh candidates from all kinds of schools. Here is what we have seen: 1. It's important when companies are hiring at scale When a company is hiring multiple fresh graduates (say 20+) a given year, they prefer to go recruit from more prestigious schools. That saves them time. It saves them time, because typically prestigious schools have a rigorous bar of intake, and a more rigorous curriculum, which translates into more candidates from these schools clearing interviews. Does it mean they all perform better at work when compared to candidates coming from other schools? No. Not by a long shot. School prestige is just an artifact of interviewing. There is in fact published research by Google, that your school and GPA only matters for first 3-4 years out of school. After that, it's all about what you do at work. 2. It's important with interviewers who have already formed biases Typically, you'll interview with several people at a company. Some of them may have formed prior biases for or against prestigious schools. This is true of recruiters, engineers, product managers as well as people managers. There is nothing you can do about it. It doesn't matter anywhere else. In fact, for engineering, more and more companies are moving to systems like HackerRank and more objective means of evaluations like GitHub profiles, in order to reduce bias.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What are the biggest mistakes engineers make when they interview?
Answer: This answer is directed towards software engineers, but some of the tips apply equally well to other engineers. The biggest strategic mistake, by far, is that the candidates interview with a loaded agony of getting a job, instead of simply demonstrating who they are. See, when you're agonizing about getting that job, you'll be nervous, you'll judge yourself during the interview, you'll amplify small mistakes, you'll fumble. But when you go there to simply explore, simply to solve a fun problem, to see how far you yourself can get, and to respect the interviewer's time, you will notice that most fumbling starts to go away. You'll take control of the interview then, because you're not agonizing. Like Bryan Cranston says: there is power in that. If you haven't watched the following clip, it's worth watching, over and over again. He is talking about actors and audition, which is very similar to interviewing: The other big strategic mistake, is actually made before the interview viz. they under-estimate the amount of preparation required. They walk into an interview like it's a lottery ticket, surprised why they didn't win it. There are some other big tactical mistakes also: 1. Not realizing that half the interview is about your communication and behavior in the interview. Had communication and behavior not been important, the companies would just send you some coding problems to do, and generate an automatic offer letter after test-cases passed. But no company does that. Why? Because they want a conversation, and you have to be ready for an inspiring conversation. 2. Trying to go for the most optimal solution from the get go, and overlooking to give the brute force. If you can't think of an optimal solution, and you don't give a brute-force solution either, the interviewer keeps wondering if you even understood the problem. Remember, that an interview is a date; it's not a standardized test. It's about showing who you are, and not about agonizing about fitting into someone's mould. You will make far less mistakes when you recognize the true nature of the beast. [I run Coding Interview Bootcamp for a living. We help candidates prepare to crack into some of the best tech companies]

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What do Indian software engineers and students who come to the US for higher studies/jobs overlook in their careers?
Answer: The biggest thing overlooked, is ironically, higher studies. Getting into US is far easier as a student than nearly any other means. Often hence, the primary purpose of many (but not all) Indian students coming to US for higher studies, is to get a clean legal entry into the US, followed by a decent job. This leads to several cascaded choices, which are all career-limiting: 1. They often opt for easy or job-oriented courses, to maintain a good GPA. There is little deliberation and/or long-term thinking and/or personal choice.  2. They mostly hang out in their own groups, leading to a feeble and narrow network after graduation. 3. They don't participate much in extra-curricular activities (especially outside their culture). 4. They rush to get a job. Many many succumb to body shops, and end up as hourly contractors doing trivial configuration and scripting on outdated tools. It's often too late before they realize that this was a permanently career-limiting move. My 2 cent advice: It's okay to take this route to come to US. But make full use of your time in college. Network generously, make deliberate choices in your coursework, participate without fear, shun the body shops, and prepare hard to get into the best companies (big or small) of your time. Name: Soham Mehta
Question: How do I prepare for a software engineering job interview?
Answer: As Paul Bryant very eloquently says: “Everyone wants to win, but very few want to prepare to win.” Ironically, the best way to prepare for a software engineering job interview is not to explicitly prepare for it. What I mean is that you should always be prepared. Software engineering is a field that changes very rapidly. Companies come and go very fast (relative to many other industries), and what's lucrative today may not be so tomorrow. If you've built a career in the field, you will want to switch jobs every 3-4 years, and hence you need to be interview-ready. To keep yourself interview-ready, practice coding and real interview problems every week/every day, even when you are not looking. Practice alone or with friends, on paper or a computer, hard problems or easy problems, this website or that Bootcamp - it doesn't matter, as long as you keep practicing without making excuses. If you need to practice in a limited amount of time, then: 0. Have a clear idea of the companies you're targeting Not all interview processes are created equal. Not all companies believe in the same processes. You should shortlist companies you want to try first. Then find out as much as you can about their interview processes. 1. Pick and stick to one programming language in your practice Get good at one and stick to it. Throughout the practice and your interviews. Don't hedge your programming language bets. 2. Get structure Depending on the time, your geography, budget, inclination, and learning style, there are many options in the market: Coding (Data Structures and Algorithms questions): Books: Elements of Programming Interviews, Cracking the Coding Interview (2011 book) Websites: LeetCode, Interview Cake, InterviewBit, GeeksforGeeks Bootcamps: http://interviewkickstart.com (Yours truly runs this one) Systems Design/Architectural design/Object Modeling questions Books: Elements of Programming Interviews, Cracking the Coding Interview (2011 book) Websites: HiredInTech (not for Object Modeling, though) Bootcamps: http://interviewkickstart.com (Yours truly runs this one) Behavioral questions Countless books, websites, and coaches, and of course, the obligatory http://interviewkickstart.com. 3. Prefer to do multiple rounds breadth-first, instead of depth-first Do a few problems in each topic (assuming you have the structure from above) in a round-robin manner. e.g., do a few on Linked Lists, then on trees, and then come back to Linked Lists. Why? Because everything builds on each other. 4. Get feedback from practice interviews Two things about practice interviews: 1. Don't do them without preparation 2. Do them only with experienced interviewers e.g., practice some 20 problems with binary trees, and then do a mock interview who knows this stuff inside and out. Feedback received after focused preparation from an experienced interviewer is far more actionable than feedback received with random practice. 5. Get a support system and believe in practice Realize that learning is a step function, not linear, i.e., you won't be twice as good at 10 problems compared to what you were at 5 problems. Unless you're born with an IQ of 140+, your only way to get better is with practice. If you stop believing in practice, you'll give up easily and not reach your goal. It's a patient climb, often up-to 400-500 problems. There is no shortcut. Get a support system of like-minded folks and mentors. Try to get multiple mentors with different backgrounds to avoid group-think. 6. Make sure you're preparing to be a good engineer, not just a good interviewee Because any experienced interviewer will tell very quickly which category you fall into. In other words, practice every problem with the intent of learning and not performing. With proper intent, you will be able to ask better questions, learn better, and perform better. Good luck [See some of my other answers on similar topics here: https://www.quora.com/Soham-Mehta-1/answers]

Question: I have a job offer from Uber and Facebook. Which one should I choose?
Answer: I've made similar decisions myself and these days I regularly deal with such questions from candidates that come to Coding Interview Bootcamp. Firstly, realize that this is not a short term decision. i.e. you cannot make it based on things like quality of perks offered. You have to make it based on the team you're joining, work culture, tech-stack and mission of the company. The latter things are going to dictate your learning and future marketability. Assuming the pay is not very different between two offers, following is the (almost) cascading decision framework we use for such tough decisions. I hope you'll find it useful. 1. Think about the Mission: Five year look-back Do you naturally connect with the mission of either company? Both are very vested in what they are doing. Imagine yourself spending five years and looking back: would you be more proud to have contributed to Facebook's mission or Uber's mission? (Are you clear about their missions?). If there is a clear answer here, then make your choice, shut your mind, and relax. If there is not a clear answer here, then keep reading. 2. Team and work Are you getting to work with similar high-caliber teams that contribute to core product? If not, then is there a team that's clearly stronger and more important to that company? Then go with that. You could say that it's easy to switch teams within a company, but you cannot take your career decision based on that hypothetical. First team you join anywhere is very important, because that brand sticks with you. 3. Risk appetite for potential financial gain If teams are similar, then ask what is your risk appetite. Uber is a higher-risk play, with a potential for a higher financial reward (like other answers have noted). Facebook is past that point. By this time, you should have a more clear idea of your decision. If you still don't, then go to next step :-) 4. Use Regret Minimization Framework See this 2-minute clip from Jeff Bezos. Question: Is it bad to use built-in language features in technical interviews??
Answer: In an interview, half of it is about the chemistry between you and the interviewer. When you do what you just said, then an interviewer could feel a mix of the following: 1. You are making fun of the interview question and hence indirectly you are making fun of me and the company I work at. 2. You are arrogant/childish. You probably already knew what you were supposed to do, but you are still not doing it. 3. You are not a very curious person. You didn't have the curiosity to learn how something as basic like that works, or even to read about how interviewing works. Now, if you get a seasoned interviewer, they will get past these feelings and politely nudge you to implement the algorithm (e.g. "You are right! Could you tell me how reverse works? Have you looked it up before? Yes? Great; please explain. No? That's okay! Let's try to implement it now!"). If you don't get a seasoned interviewer, then it won't matter if you are right or wrong. They will have mentally already rejected you. At least, your score would fall in their eyes. Deeper question you may be asking, is why do they expect you to dive deeper with such questions? A few reasons for that: 1. An urge to dive beyond the surface level is a strong indicator of your interest in the career you have chosen to pursue. The less black-boxes you mentally have, the better you are likely to succeed in that area. 2. If they simply wanted someone who could cobble functions and APIs together, they'd hire a pair of hands to do C++ for cheap (there are many avenues to do that). They don't what that. They want a mind to come with that pair of hands. A mind that is excited to dig deeper to get a better understanding of things. 3. If it's a company worth working for, then they are simply getting a lot of qualified applicants for the same position. They hence have to find some way to filter candidates out. If you stop at writing in-built functions, you can, but I bet that they'll get someone else who will not question their judgement, write what was expected of them, and get that job.

Question: How can I increase my income as a software engineer over the years? I have around 12 years of experience, but my salary is almost stagnant over these 12 years.
Answer: You can't increase your salary by much; but what you can do, is increase your overall payout. At the risk of getting downvoted into oblivion, I'm going to give you this unpopular advice: Move to Silicon Valley and join a fast-growing startup. Philip Su is absolutely right, when he says, that you are only worth your replacement cost. Like Philip, I've also managed several engineers and that's how the world works. There is not a great way for you to break out of that. You're going to maintain that salary in the ballpark (inflation adjusted, location adjusted) till you retire. e.g. if you move to the valley and work for Google, you may be paid ~200K, but adjusted for Valley, that's not a big jump. Make sure you hang on to that 401K. Alternatively, you can take a step back and realize this: you are in a field (high-end programming), that has the potential of a windfall money every few years. Outside of Investment Banking (and of course Entrepreneurship), there is no other field, that has that potential. (Doctors don't make windfalls; they just make steady good salaries). The way to make a windfall, is to join a fast-growing startup early. Early equity gives you a windfall when the startup "exits" a few years later. How do you know if a startup is going to be successful? You don't. Advice abounds about how startup payout as an employee is a myth. But most people who say that, forget that you don't have to hit a windfall with every startup, just like a VC doesn't have to make money from every startup they invest in. You only need one or two windfalls in your career, just the way a VC needs only one or two unicorns in their portfolio. Also, these days, startups worth their salt actually pay market salaries, so you don't lose on that either. So even if you lucked out once after 4 or 5 startups, it'll surpass the cumulative money you'll make as an employee working for replacement wage. What is the guarantee that you'll hit a successful startup even in 4 or 5 tries? None, in theory. BUT, don't forget that as you work for startups, you'll learn a lot about how startups work and which ones to pick. A lot of things will get abundantly clear e.g. types of founders, types of equity structures, what to negotiate, what investors to look for, what are the red flags, what are good signs, when to leave and most importantly, your own strengths and weaknesses. What is the guarantee that you'll learn these things? 100%. That's because learning is a survival trait; if you are exposed to the same thing over and over again, you'll start to learn even if you don't want to. In Silicon Valley, such success stories happen every day, even if you may not want to believe it. It's more common than the random articles on the Internet make you believe. Good luck.

Question: If algorithmic problem solving is what they want to test, why don't they hire top-rated Top Coder or Codeforces directly?
Answer: It is true, that Competitive Programming is very challenging and doing enough of it makes you much better at solving algorithmic problems in interviews (and at work). But it's different enough in some key aspects, that valuing it so highly to simply hire competitive programmers directly doesn't make much sense: Primary reason: Companies are not primarily looking for algorithmic coders Companies spend hundreds of hours interviewing and looking for the right candidates. If we wanted to test just algorithmic problem solving, there are many easier ways to do it. Giving out offers to TopCoders is one. Sending coding challenges is another. Just write code, let the test-cases pass and voila! you have an offer in your hand! But what we really want to gauge, is if we can work with you, if you'll fit the culture, if you have the right experience etc. We want to have a conversation with you. A problem is just a means to that conversation. So if it's primarily about conversing, then why take an algorithmically challenging problem? Why not talk about fantasy sports or that popular soap-opera or the late-night show or even weather? Because that's not the culture. The culture (culture of a growing tech company) demands strong technical fundamentals too. Giving an algorithmically challenging problem kills two birds at one stone. Other reasons 1. Competitive Programming is all-or-nothing In competitive programming, it's about all or nothing i.e. either all test-cases pass and you get full points (and you win), or you don't (and you lose). Interviews are not that binary. When we're looking at your thought-process, it's okay to not solve a question as fully - as long as the interviewer likes your thought process, you can still get the job. And quite likely you'll carry that thought-process to actual work and succeed there. 2. Competitive programming values only one thing: speed. Competitive Programming values one and only one thing: speed (with accuracy assumed). Doesn't really value code-readability, choice of programming language paradigms, trade-offs of choosing one data-structure over the other, code reviews, testability, coding standards and guidelines etc. In actual work, while speed is important, it's not overly important; we care a lot about other things in your code. e.g. I and most managers would be fine if my engineers took half a day to implement a Trie. As long as it's the right solution, it's implemented efficiently, your code is readable, well-tested, well-reviewed, and within the guidelines of the codebase (again, accuracy is assumed), it doesn't really matter that you took more than 45 minutes to write it. Hope this helps. Disclaimer: This topic is "Google Interview Questions". I have never worked for Google. But by way of my background, by way of running a meetup on Competitive Programming in the valley and my business, I'm intimately familiar with interviewing processes of many tech companies of the valley.

Question: Where can I find a large collection of programming interview questions with answers categorized by difficulty?
Answer: There is no one single place that will give you what you want. Realize that it's impossible for such a place to exist. Why? 0. Programming is a vast topic, with several languages, stacks and biases. 1. Interview questions can be just made up on the fly. It's easy to convert anything into a programming problem. 2. Difficulty is a subjective matter (i.e. what may be difficult for me, may not be difficult for you). 3. Categorization is subjective. e.g. For a problem like QuickSort, would you put it in Arrays? In Sorting? In Recursion? 4. It's very hard to curate the questions, remove duplicates etc. You'll need to solve every incoming question to be able to do so properly. 5. Internet is a free-form medium. Even if I have such a site, you'll want your own, because you can! For my business , I've scoured many resources and I continue to do so. I'll list them here, with my subjective comments on some. Remember, that my selection is solely based on an interviewing viewpoint only, not from an algorithms class viewpoint or even from a competitive programming viewpoint. Sources that I like the most Online source: http://GeeksForGeeks.org . It's the closest to a curated site that you'll get. It's not perfect, but I've been impressed with their breadth and answers. They have not categorized it by difficulty though. Book: Elements of Programming Interviews I really like this book. It is very organized and has a lot of good interview problems, which are also practical. They do have a category of challenging problems. It's a bit theoretical, but if you take the time to persist, then it is understandable. A close second: Book: Cracking the Coding Interview (2011 book) It has fewer problems than the one above, but is also more interview-oriented than that book. Problems are a bit less challenging though. Site: saurabhschool This is not organized by difficulty, but has a pretty large collection of questions. Almost like the EPI book, but with video talks. More excellent ones: 0. Book: Introduction to Algorithms Doesn't have Interview Questions per se, but is categorized extremely well and is meant for learning from scratch. 1.
