Name: Soham Mehta
Question: What are your greatest frustrations/challenges when studying data structures/algorithms and prepping for technical interviews? What are your biggest roadblocks to learning and retaining knowledge?
Answer: Congratulations. Everyone keeps complaining that algorithms and Data Structures are hard, but very few dig deeper to ask why. And only those who do, actually get better at it (or actually can help get others better at it). Let's think about it, shall we? First of all, let's realize that learning in itself, is a problem in NP. i.e. while it's possible to verify whether you've learnt something in a bounded, explainable (polynomial) amount of time, nobody really knows how to achieve learning. The teaching community has their best empirical guesses crystallized over a period of time, but there is no theoretical universal systematic pattern that has been established. i.e. you won't be able to tell me today with 100% certainty, that if you read/do X and Y, you will learn Z. You'll be able to test me on Z and be clearly be able to tell if I have learnt Z, but you won't be able to tell how I exactly got there, and be able to replicate that pattern with others. That's just how complex each human mind is. Now back to the questions: you are asking three separate but related, very good questions here: Question 1: What do you feel are the biggest roadblocks to learning and retaining knowledge, understanding, and implementation details of algorithms and data structures? I first-hand connect with this problem from several angles. I've had trouble learning algorithms, I've had trouble in hiring engineers, I've had trouble in preparing candidates for CS interviews AND I've had trouble in finding instructors who can do so. I divide the roadblocks into two categories: A. System Roadblocks and B. Thinking Roadblocks A. System Roadblocks aka Roadblocks in setting up a system of learning. The key to learning anything new (especially cognitively challenging tasks like Algorithms), is to persist with it for long enough time, under proper guidance, with challenging curriculum and motivated peers. That system is probably more important than the topic itself. If you are in the right school, then you get all of that in a package. If you're not, then all those things become roadblocks. Roadblock-1: Finding engineers/teachers who can give proper guidance Books are a great source, but having someone knowledgeable to ask questions is critical to speedy and long-term learning. And of course, by definition, there are aren't that many people who know Algos/DS stuff well enough, that they can guide others. Roadblock-2: Finding peers who want to learn it with the same seriousness We all know, that learning something together is not only fun, it's also fast and we retain things longer. But having the right partner is important. You need someone who is at the same level as you, and is committed just like you are. Otherwise it's a serious waste of time and leads to demotivation. Roadblock-3: Absence of enough real-world projects There are not many real world projects today that require you to select or implement algorithms or DS. (Why? See one of my answers Soham Mehta's answer to I've been coding for some time now and have developed several web applications. I haven't used any algorithms or even much math. I haven't done any of the complicated things that are so often talked about in computer science. Why?) When you are not faced with many real-world applications of what you're learning, it's very easy to get demotivated. Not to mention, that without an existential pressure to do something, it's very hard to learn something new properly. A hitler parody is in order:  B. Thinking Roadblocks (or frustrations) Roadblock-4: Too much exposure to linear thinking The way humans learn, they associate everything new with something that's very familiar to them. The real world forces us to think linearly all day, because that's how nearly everything works. viz. this happens after that, 4 comes after 3, etc. When it comes to Algos and DS though, there is much more than linear thinking. There is looping, there is recursion, there are trees and then there is memoization. All of these are not very natural constructs for the world that's mostly linear. But we have a habit of associating every Algo/DS linearly, which holds us back (roadblock). That's why you'll notice that most people are good with Arrays and Linked Lists, but complain about nearly everything else. Roadblock-5: Not having cultivated mathematical thinking What is mathematical thinking? Mathematical thinking (not necessarily mathematics) makes a lot of CS easier. Mathematical thinking is about recognizing patterns. It's about organizing your thoughts to create something. e.g. Take the question: what is the sum of positive integers from 1 through N? This is high-school math. But if one doesn't remember the formula, then one should be able to derive it. The moment you put 1 thru N on the board, a pattern should jump out, leading you to the answer. Such thinking only develops thru proper grade-schooling and again, deliberate effort. A lack of it makes CS learning slow, and Algorithmic/Data-Structure interviews even slower. Roadblock-6: Not enough patience/time Learning anything new needs you to struggle with it, break your world views and then wrestle it down to the ground. Many people don't have the time or patience to do so. Roadblock-7: Not enough revision Recall is as important as learning. IOW, it's not enough to just learn something; it's also enough to practice recalling it, or you may not be able to recall it when the time comes. Revision and repetition are key. Roadblock-8: Rarely, some people just don't have the mind for it See this study if you haven't: Hitting the High Notes "The quality of the work and the amount of time spent are simply uncorrelated." Quesion-2: Why do so many interviewees have trouble with technical interviews? Assuming this question is limited to Algos and DS, the answer to this now becomes simple: 1. They haven't studied CS properly in college They have CS degrees (bachelors, masters, doesn't matter), but they coasted for the most part, doing just enough to pass the exams and maintain a GPA. They did not take time to really persist through difficult problems. They did not surround themselves with peers who would study together and challenge each other. Their teachers did not pay enough attention either. A great example is understanding of Recursion. Most people struggle with recursion when they do it first, but only those who persist through several problems, internalize it and retain it for a long time. 2. OR once they are out of school, they have not been able to overcome the roadblocks mentioned above See the list of roadblocks identified above. Most people want to win, but they don't have the will to prepare to win i.e. the will to remove the roadblocks to winning. 3. They have practiced properly, but the company hasn't thought properly about their interviewing process Many interviewers tend to ask what they know, vs. what's required for the job. If the interviewee is not in the interviewer's window of knowledge, then they will be perceived as lacking. This often happens with inexperienced interviewers. Yet another set of interviewers don't put in enough effort in picking out questions that are relevant for the job. They treat interviewing like it's intellectual perversion. Many companies don't have a culture of paying attention to interviewing. See one of my other answers here: Can candidates in programming interviews really write code on the spot?  Also, a Dilbert strip is in order: Dilbert comic strip for 02/14/1993 from the official Dilbert comic strips archive. 4. They are a mismatch from the get-go Some just pick wrong companies to interview with, even though their backgrounds don't match. Companies also overlook this fact quite often. e.g. if I interview at a Semiconductor company, it's not likely that I'll pass that interview. Question 3, the one you're really asking: Why wouldn't interviewees learn Algos and DS and prepare for interviews? 1. They don't know or can't admit, that they will have to practice Best way to practice, is to keep working a little bit on the side while you're on the job and that it can be done. See some amazing answers to this question: How can I get a job at Facebook or Google in 6 months? I need a concise work-plan to build a good enough skill set. Should I join some other start-up or build my own projects/start-up? Should I just focus on practicing data structures and algorithms? If they knew or admitted, they'd look for ways to make it happen. 2. They prepare, but not deliberately Anything you need to get good at, needs Deliberate Practice. Interviews are no different. In order to confidently prepare before walking into a challenging interview, one needs to do some of the following things: a. Time himself/herself when coding b. Do mock interviews c. Work on the right programming problems (not too easy, progressively harder) d. Work with a teacher or an expert who can guide e. Follow a process that encourages recall as effectively as learning of new concepts f. Struggling with difficult problems until they are completely solved g. Have the right solutions to learn from and apply to h. Have the right, optimistic mindset i. Do enough number of problems j. Be in similar company and exchange ideas k. Read the right books and prior work As you can see, a lot of things need to come together to overcome difficulties and increase retention. 3. They prepare, but not with a competitive mindset In an interview, it's not enough to be good at Algorithms and DS. You also have to be competitively good i.e. solve those problems under time-pressure. Interviews are a competition. But most daily programming jobs don't require you to program competitively in a time-bound manner. Programmers are not athletes; they are creative people. But interviewing is meant for athletes. That's because as a hiring manager, I only have budget for one position and only so much time. I'm hence going to make all the candidates run (program) as fluently as they can in a given amount of time. Which means, that to succeed in that race, one needs to practice competitively on the side, to keep up with fast thinking. And most people are either unaware or too lazy to do that. 4. They are practicing, but are using your interviews to "practice" Some candidates knowingly do "practice" interviews with companies they don't care much about, before they interview with their favorite companies. 5. They overvalue their experience Research has shown for a number of years, that software engineering is not a field where experience necessarily turns into expertise. World is divided into two kinds of tech companies: Ones that deal with Scale (Google, Facebook, Twitter etc.) and ones that don't. (Scale == Millions of users). The former kind deal with enough challenging problems, that needs their engineers to pay enough attention to every part of the code. Otherwise, the site gets very slow and grinds to a halt. Those engineers end up getting exposed to several algorithmic techniques and data-structures in that environment, and hence have bit of an easier time interviewing outside. Not to mention that they also get exposure to such interview questions where they work. Working at companies (or teams) that don't deal with Scale does make for well paying careers, but often doesn't expose you to problems challenging enough to warrant a better data-structure and algorithm. Candidates coming from those companies hence, often struggle. If you have not been working at a company that throws such problems at you every day, there is no chance you're going to do well in interviews without explicit practice. 6. They think it's okay to be good-enough, and high demand will work in their favor The demand for tech talent is just so high. Most people know that they are going to find something or the other, so they don't care if they fail a few interviews. It may not be at your company; but some other company. That reflects in their performance in your interviews. They hence try to throw a lot of spaghetti on the wall to see what sticks. -- Phew! That got a little too long. Hopefully it's useful!

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Can candidates in programming interviews really write code on the spot?
Answer: Summary: You are not a bad programmer. Technical interviewing has become a game of intellectual perversion, instead of really finding out what the candidate knows, and what is their potential. And that's because it's the path of least resistance that humans so succumb to. So don't ever penalize yourself with such negative thoughts. Explanation: Most interviewers in Tech don't give enough thought to what they are asking and how relevant it is to the job in question. When they are looking for interview questions, they get excited with the intellectual rush they get with all such problems out there. After spending some time on these questions at their leisure, they rationalize their choice and their time spent, with lame arguments like: "I don't want to hire anyone who can't think of XOR in 30 minutes!" "If I interview elsewhere, I get asked the same kind of questions!" "Everybody asks these questions!" etc, even if the job is never going to require dealing with XOR. The hiring panel needs to give a lot of continuous thought on what skills and level of aptitude is required for various jobs and then they need to find appropriate questions for that role. e.g. If you're interviewing at a place which deals with a ton of bit-manipulation at low level, then expecting you to know the properties of XOR is a fair game. Similarly, if you are interviewing with a team that mucks with a Linux-like kernel, then questions on Red Black trees are fair too. But giving this kind of thought is hard, takes time to improvise and perfect, and takes time away from things of immediate gratification. It's not a path of least resistance. Path of least resistance is to pick a tricky/hard question from the Internet (because everyone asks those), rationalize it and be done with it. In my mind, hence, it's not a judgment on you; it's a judgement on the process itself. So what can you do? A few things: 1. Try and interview with companies that pay a lot of attention to their interviewing processes. (Box, my previous company for example, did). Ask your friends. You may not be able to find many, but you at least try. 2. Practice and practice more. If you simply do two such problems a day, you'll have eventually done enough problems in 3 months, that you won't worry about this anymore. 3. Wherever you get hired, urge them to pay a lot more attention to their interviewing process. Volunteer to set and manage that process on an ongoing basis (nobody wants to do that, even though it's so important).

Question: I've been coding for some time now and have developed several web applications. I haven't used any algorithms or even much math. I haven't done any of the complicated things that are so often talked about in computer science. Why?
Answer: Jeff Darcy nails it. At any given time, either you are working with commonly-used systems that have abstracted the complexity for you (e.g. Databases), or if you are writing custom systems, then they are not at a scale where agonizing over fast algorithms and custom data-structures is required. I often advice this to the candidates that come to me: The tech world is divided into two kinds of companies. The companies that deal with scale and companies that don't. Best learning and best salaries come by working with the former.

Question: How can I get a job at Facebook or Google in 6 months? I need a concise work-plan to build a good enough skill set. Should I join some other start-up or build my own projects/start-up? Should I just focus on practicing data structures and algorithms?
Answer: (Thanks for A2A, User-10268054657760936088) There are some really really good answers here. Great read. I've answered a similar question elsewhere, which may give you some good food for thought: Soham Mehta's answer to I am planning to quit my job and study algorithms full-time for one year. My target is to train my algorithms skill for preparing a Google interview. Can anyone give me some advice? While many interviewers at Google do care about the language you pick to program (Python, C++ or Java), that is not what they care about the most. They care about CS fundamentals, and more importantly, your fluency in those fundamentals. Whichever plan you make and follow, the most important thing, IMHO, is to do your preparation in "breadth-first" order and continually measure yourself after each round. That will help you know when to stop, and expose your strengths and weaknesses more quickly. Good luck.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: I am planning to quit my job and study algorithms full-time for one year. My target is to train my algorithms skill for preparing a Google interview. Can anyone give me some advice?
Answer: Congratulations on that thought. It's a bold idea, and I commend you for even thinking about it; not many can. Everyone wants to win, but very few want to prepare to win. As founder of Coding Interview Bootcamp, Interview Kickstart , I routinely talk to engineers who aspire to get into some of the best companies in Silicon Valley. [BTW, we're enrolling for upcoming batches!] Most of them don't have the luxury of spending a year full-time on it. But if you do, that's awesome and the following is what I'd advice you: Short version: IMHO, quitting or not is a secondary decision. Your primary decision is to figure out what you will do with your time, such that it maximizes your chances to achieve your goal. Longer version: (Longer version got longer than what I'd thought I'd initially write, but I hope that anyone who reads it will find it useful): 1. Make a meticulous plan The plan you've given is a good start, but go deeper with that. What you need, is a plan for Deliberate Practice. Read all about Deliberate Practice and I bet it'll resonate with you. You want to exactly know how many days you'll take off, how many hours you can put into it per day, how many topics you'll study and how many projects or interview-problems (roughly) you want to get exposed to, per topic. And you want to do this prep with interview-orientation. Cracking the Coding Interview (2011 book) is a very good book, but depending on the team you interview at Google, you may not find it adequate. I'd say also go thru Elements of Programming Interviews book. Between those two books and Glassdoor (company), you should have enough fodder. You can also use Introduction to Algorithms (book by Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein), but I'd suggest you use it more as a reference, instead of an interview-prep book, otherwise you may get overwhelmed. On the same lines, I am not sure if an Algorithms class is going to be very useful. It may be useful as a system of discipline (see my next point), but not super useful for interview prep. They're likely to cover a lot of material that's not interview-useful, and not give enough practice on material that actually is. When you're practicing problems, make sure to write code. Code every problem you study, and time yourself. If you exceed 45 minutes in any problem, then do it again and again until you bring it down to 45 minutes. Use TopCoder or Codeforces or HackerRank or LeetCode or similar to practice a bit more competitively. Many people will advise you to practice on a whiteboard instead of coding. While that definitely helps and is required, getting fluent with writing algorithms and data-structures in actual code is the first step. Once you are comfortable with that, then transferring that skill to a whiteboard is not much work. Point being, when you make a detailed plan, is when you'll know what to do next, and it will feed into your go/no-go decision. 2. It may not take a full year How will you know that you're ready? a. Go breadth-first, instead of depth-first. With the help of someone, decide on a set of topics you need to practice (Arrays, Strings, Recursion, DP, Trees etc),. Then divide your plan into progressively deeper phases with more challenging interview-problems. Do a measured bit of all topics in each phase instead of devoting a phase to an entire topic. Again - don't forget to write code for each problem you study. b. Measure yourself with mock interviews after each phase. When you see yourself improving in mock interviews, you'll get more confident. You'll know when to stop and it's very likely that you may not need a full year. Make sure you find the right interviewers to do mock interviews. Good interviewing is a function of experience in interviewing. In order to justify the time off on the resume, I'd advice you to do some freelancing work on the side. 3. Create a support system If you are as human as most humans are, then keeping focus, discipline and motivation through your year off (or even part-time) is going to be hard. Very hard. In order to keep that adrenalin up, you should create the best support system you can, with some or all of the following a. Create a system of study: Nobody says it better than Scott Adams does. Read this, patiently: Scott Adams Blog (Goals vs Systems). b. Find a buddy: Study together, check each other's work, hold each other accountable. You both will retain the knowledge longer and grow stronger together. Did you know, that CS colleges in Israel give joint homework? It often works like magic. c. Find a mentor (or mentors): Someone who already works at Google and trusts you for what you are, would be great. Ask for guidance, mock interviews, evaluations, code-reviews etc. d. Measure yourself, constantly: After every sub-goal achieved, make sure to evaluate/judge/measure yourself with some objective measure e.g. a mock interview or a coding challenge. e. Health insurance: If you have a partner who can support you, that's awesome. If not, you need to factor in Obamacare premium as part of your savings (US only, of course). 4. Work for mastery, not to crack Google Counter intuitive as it may sound, but it is the most important thing: Don't aim for Google. Aim to get mastery over interview algorithms/data-structures. Google will follow. When you gain mastery, then many others companies will follow too. Working for Mastery vs Performance is a well-known theory in education. When you aim for Mastery vs. Performance is when you'll be able to pull yourself out of low moments. And only then, a lot of things I suggested earlier will become easy viz. writing code, timing yourself, doing mock interviews, talking with like-minded people etc. 5. Interview mastery will translate into superior performance at work. That's hard to believe, but I've seen that happen in several cases. Interview Questions are a great means to learn. They are the fastest connectors of theory and practice. They expose you to real challenges and make you think harder. Most importantly, you'll not be worried about finding a job again, which will make you more confident at your current work. 6. Continually measure yourself Repeating and highlighting this point, because I can't emphasize this enough. Mock interviews are a great way to measure your progress. Do a round before you start and do a round after each phase of your prep. That way, you'll know when to stop and how far to go. There is no other way you'll objectively know. 7. Clearly know what you are optimizing for Realize that this is an expensive experiment for you. Not only you'll spend your savings of a year, you'll also lose the salary for a year. If you are in Silicon Valley, that can easily mean $200K total, after tax. Even if you join Google, you'll take about 2 years to recover that kind of money. Though of course, money isn't the only thing that matters and there are many other intangible benefits of cracking into best companies. I just mean that you should have a good sense of that overall, and be comfortable with it. Lastly: Your last line is spot on and shows your great attitude. Interviews are neither exact science, nor standardized tests, and there is more to it beyond algorithms and data-structures. So you may still fail at Google interviews after all this. But if you've worked with the aim of gaining mastery, and utilized every waking moment of that year with a plan, you will still come out ahead, and your prep will benefit you in unseen ways. It has to. If you decide to take the plunge, then I wish you the very best. Like they say, May the force be with you! (Prepare to win quote adapted from a similar quote by Paul Bryant) (Edit 1: Highlighted some important concerns that were buried Edit 2: Added a short version, and attributed the quote)

Question: How does Aaron Levie feel knowing he is down to a 4% stake heading into the Box IPO?
Answer: I believe that there is a lot more than what meets the eye in the S1. 1. In all likelihood, Aaron might have come ahead of any single person/partner/family who invested in Box. Realize that DFJ is a representing VC firm for it's Limited Partners (LPs). And likely several LPs invested in multiple funds, which funded Box over the years. Given how popular Box is, it's unlikely that only one or two LPs formed the fund that invested in Box. It must have been several LPs, which means no single LP probably owns more than 5% of Box. In fact, they probably faced several more failed companies to find one Box. I don't know what management fees Draper Fisher Jurvetson (venture capital firm) charges, but if it's about the standard 2/20, then probably they are the only entity that made more than Levie, though not significantly more. 2. Realize that Aaron started Box when he was ~20. If you're getting money from a top VC firm at that age, you'd be tempted to do anything to make that happen. It's hard to have enough bargaining power without enough prior credibility, especially with smart people. 3. Money is merely one dimension of keeping score in startups (and in life). There are many others you will judge yourself by (or others will). Satisfaction of building a successful company in the Valley is far more than getting lucky investing in it. As an angel investor, I can attest to it first hand. 4. When Aaron starts his next venture, who do you think is going to keep the lion's share? Remember that he is not even 30.

Name: Soham Mehta
Question: Which major countries (or cities) have populations who have a tradition of eating out infrequently?
Answer: In my case, I grew up in a fairly middle-class family in India and eating out frequently was simply unaffordable. A decent sit-down restaurant would cost about a percentage of my Dad's income in a single meal for 4 people. And he had a decently paying job in a bank. Another reason we didn't like eating out, was because in most restaurants, the food wasn't perceived to be that "good quality". It would be argued that the chefs will never take the time out to pick quality vegetables, grains and spices, that they would be looking for bulk discounts on cheap stuff to maximize the margins. Eating out frequently hence was (and probably still is) associated with bad health longer term. Yet another reason, is simply cultural, where moms are expected to and love to feed home-cooked food to their kids every day. My mom did that even though she worked a full-time job. As a result of these habits, we still cook most of our meals at home, even though it has been 12 years we migrated to US. My wife works a fulltime job, and she still cooks daily meals. We watch our spending when we eat out, and we don't trust most restaurants :-) And that's unlikely to change.
